nodes.bodyText:
# opencode-ai-context-plugin

A native [OpenCode](https://opencode.ai) plugin that gives the agent a local,
Docker-free code index (indexing and search run locally; see the data boundary below): semantic search, repository structure, call/import
impact analysis and document search. It replaces the Docker-based MCP server,
LSP bridge and file watcher of this repo's `.ai-context/` stack.

Each multi-chunk file also gets an L1 summary chunk, written by a local
OpenAI-compatible LLM (LM Studio, Ollama, oMLX; configure `summary_llm`) and
falling back to a deterministic summary when none is reachable (rewritten
automatically once the LLM answers; `reindex_summaries` forces it). Search combines
vectors with FTS5 BM25 and a small cross-encoder re-ranker; other indexed repos
can be searched via an allowlist.

Works in the opencode TUI and under ACP (JetBrains AI Assistant). The embedding
model runs in one shared background process, so the opencode host stays small.

> **Data boundary:** indexing, embeddings and search run locally, but the
> plugin cannot control what the agent does with the results. Retrieved code
> and documents become part of the conversation and go to your configured model
> provider, which may not be local. See [docs/data-boundary.md](docs/data-boundary.md).

children.title: Quickstart
children.summary: The Quickstart guide provides instructions for installing and configuring the search index plugin for opencode. It covers setting up the environment, enabling the plugin, and following the indexing process.
children.bodyText:
## Quickstart

```bash
npm install
npm run build
./scripts/install-plugin.sh
```

Restart opencode. The plugin is opt-in per repository: the generated
`.opencode/ai-context.config.yaml` has `enabled: false`; set it to `true` and
restart. The first index takes minutes; follow it in
`.opencode/ai-context/index-status.json`. Next to it: `index-tree.md` (which files are indexed, with date/repo/branch) and `error.log.md` (what failed and why). More: [docs/installation.md](docs/installation.md).

The plugin relies on opencode's native `lsp` tool. opencode only registers it
when `OPENCODE_EXPERIMENTAL_LSP_TOOL=true` is set in the environment that
starts opencode (setting it from inside the plugin may come too late).

Indexing follows file changes through opencode's file watcher, which is opt-in
(`OPENCODE_EXPERIMENTAL_FILEWATCHER`). The plugin sets that flag itself (best
effort, same caveat; export it too if `index_status` shows `watcher.eventsReceived: 0`).
Because the watcher can stay silent, the plugin also rescans the repo shortly after
`bash`/`write`/`edit` calls, and `ai_context_rescan` does it on demand. Fingerprints skip
unchanged files, so a rescan is cheap.

## Status

Accepted (2026-09). Implemented incrementally; see the sibling ADRs for
individual component decisions.

children.title: Context
children.summary: The documentation covers the original `.ai-context/` tooling, which ran as a multi-container Docker stack with Postgres+Qdrant, StreamableHTTP, and language servers. It discusses the decision to replace this tooling with `sst/opencode`, which provides native equivalents for semantic code search, call/import-graph analysis, and long-document navigation.
children.bodyText:
## Context

`.ai-context/` (the parent monorepo's original tooling) ran as a
multi-container Docker stack: a Postgres+Qdrant-backed MCP server
exposed over StreamableHTTP, a standalone file watcher container doing
continuous delta re-indexing, and an `lsp-bridge` container wrapping
several language servers (Python, Swift, clangd) behind a custom
protocol. All of this existed to give a coding agent semantic code
search, call/import-graph analysis, and long-document navigation.

By 2026, `sst/opencode` (the agent runtime this repo's users actually
run) had grown built-in equivalents for several of those
responsibilities: a native `lsp` tool with on-demand
`incomingCalls`/`outgoingCalls`/`findReferences`, native `grep`/`glob`,
a `skill` mechanism, and a first-class plugin API with `tool`,
`event`, and `config` hooks. Running a separate Docker stack alongside
an agent runtime that already covers much of the same ground meant:
extra operational surface (containers to start/keep healthy), a
network hop for every tool call (StreamableHTTP to a local server
instead of an in-process function call), and duplicate maintenance of
features OpenCode already had natively.

children.title: Decision
children.summary: The search index rebuilds hybrid semantic/keyword code search and precomputed call/import-graph analysis as a native OpenCode plugin, using existing tools like `grep`, `glob`, and `lsp` calls. It integrates with OpenCode's tool/event/config hooks without requiring a separate server, Docker, or watcher process.
children.bodyText:
## Decision

Rebuild the *irreplaceable* differentiators -- hybrid semantic/keyword
code search and (opt-in) precomputed call/import-graph analysis -- as a
native OpenCode plugin (`opencode-ai-context-plugin/`), registered
directly via the plugin's `tool`/`event`/`config` hooks, with no MCP
server, no Docker, no separate watcher process. Everything OpenCode
already does well natively (`grep`, `glob`, on-demand `lsp` calls,
`skill` discovery) is deliberately NOT reimplemented; the plugin's
[`docs/architecture.md`](../architecture.md) documents this
overlap explicitly rather than leaving it implicit.

children.title: Consequences
children.summary:
- No containerized setup for core workflow; `npm install` + OpenCode plugin directory is "install" step.
- Plugin calls are in-process, not network round trips.
- Plugin only runs during OpenCode sessions, re-indexing via startup reconciliation and file watcher events.
- `lsp-bridge` deleted, replaced by OpenCode's `lsp` tool.
- Capabilities dependent on stack running independently of OpenCode sessions lost.
children.bodyText:
## Consequences

- No containers to run, start, or keep healthy for the core workflow;
  `npm install` + OpenCode picking up the plugin directory is the
  entire "install" step.
- Every plugin tool call is an in-process function call, not a network
  round trip -- removes an entire latency/failure-mode class (the
  StreamableHTTP transport, connection resets, "is the MCP server up"
  health checks).
- The plugin only fires while OpenCode is actually running a session
  -- there is no always-on watcher process. Re-indexing instead happens
  via (a) a one-off startup reconciliation walk when a session begins,
  and (b) `file.watcher.updated` events for the rest of the session.
  This trades "index is always fresh, even with OpenCode closed" for
  "no standing infrastructure" -- acceptable since the plugin's whole
  purpose is serving that same running OpenCode session.
- `lsp-bridge/` (the Python LSP client wrappers + its Dockerfile) was
  deleted entirely rather than ported, since its exact capability
  (on-demand call/reference lookups) is now covered natively by
  OpenCode's own `lsp` tool -- see ADR-0006.
- Losing: any capability that depended on the stack running
  independently of an active OpenCode session (e.g. a CI job querying
  the MCP server directly). None of this repo's current use cases
  needed that, so it wasn't preserved.

children.title: Alternatives considered
children.summary: The text discusses two alternatives for a search index: keeping the Docker stack with a thin plugin or rewriting the MCP server in-process but keeping it MCP-shaped. Both alternatives were rejected due to operational overhead and unnecessary complexity.
children.bodyText:
## Alternatives considered

- **Keep the Docker stack, add a thin plugin as a client of it.**
  Rejected: this keeps 100% of the operational overhead the rewrite
  was meant to remove, for a benefit (protocol reuse) that doesn't
  matter once nothing else consumes the MCP server directly.
- **Rewrite the MCP server in-process but keep it MCP-shaped (still a
  separate transport, just no Docker).** Rejected: OpenCode's plugin
  `tool` hook already IS the in-process registration mechanism; adding
  an MCP layer on top would be a transport nobody needs.

children.title: Status
children.summary: The documentation covers the status of a search index, indicating it is accepted for storage with a spike in 2026-09.
children.bodyText:
## Status

Accepted (storage-spike, 2026-09).

children.title: Context
children.summary: The documentation covers the context of replacing a Docker-based infrastructure with an embedded, zero-server storage solution for vector search. Key terms include `better-sqlite3`, `vector search`, and `brute-force JS cosine similarity scan`.
children.bodyText:
## Context

The original stack used Postgres (structured metadata) + Qdrant (vector
search) as separate always-on services. Replacing the Docker
infrastructure (ADR-0001) meant the storage layer needed a genuinely
embedded, zero-server alternative -- something that lives inside the
plugin's own Node process with no separate service to start, healthy,
or connect to.

A storage spike measured `better-sqlite3` (synchronous, in-process,
file-backed) storing 768-dim vectors as BLOBs, with a v1 brute-force JS
cosine similarity scan (no ANN index) over all stored chunks per query.

children.title: Decision
children.summary: The search index uses `better-sqlite3` as the storage backend with brute-force cosine similarity for v1. The search latency is measured at 110ms for 2,000 chunks, 580ms for 10,000 chunks, and 1.75s for 30,000 chunks. The plugin only supports SQLite for now, and a tentative cutover point to Qdrant-backed path is 8,000 chunks.
children.bodyText:
## Decision

Use `better-sqlite3` as the sole storage backend
(`src/storage/vector-store.ts`), with brute-force cosine similarity in
JS for v1 -- no HNSW/IVF index, no separate vector database.

Measured search latency (768-dim vectors, brute-force scan):

| Chunk count | Latency |
| --- | --- |
| ~2,000 | ~110ms |
| ~10,000 | ~580ms |
| ~30,000 | ~1.75s |

This informs a tentative ~8,000-chunk threshold as a candidate cutover
point to a "heavy mode" Qdrant-backed path for very large monorepos --
**not yet implemented or validated against a real repo**; today the
plugin only has the SQLite path.

children.title: Consequences
children.summary: The search index uses a `.sqlite` file for storage, which is created lazily by the plugin process. Search latency increases linearly with chunk count, making it suitable for small/medium repos but not for very large monorepos. The storage is schema-less and connection-pool-free, with future work planned for a heavy mode cutover.
children.bodyText:
## Consequences

- Zero operational surface for storage: the `.sqlite` file lives under
  `~/.local/share/opencode-ai-context-plugin/projects/<key>/index.sqlite`,
  created/opened lazily by the plugin process itself.
- Search latency degrades linearly with chunk count since there's no
  ANN index -- acceptable for small/medium repos (the plugin's primary
  target), a real risk for very large monorepos once past roughly
  10-30k chunks.
- No externally-imposed schema/connection-pool/auth complexity that a
  real Postgres+Qdrant pair would require even for a single-user local
  tool.
- Left open, deliberately: a real "heavy mode" storage cutover (e.g.
  reintroducing Qdrant only past a measured chunk-count threshold) is
  future work, not yet built. `AI_CONTEXT_PLUGIN_HEAVY_MODE` currently
  has no effect on storage at all (see ADR-0006's note on the flag's
  scope).

children.title: Alternatives considered
children.summary: The text discusses two alternatives considered for a search index: running Qdrant out-of-process and using an embedded vector index library. The first alternative was rejected outright by ADR-0001 due to reintroducing the exact operational overhead being removed. The second alternative was deferred rather than rejected, as adding complexity (another native binding and index-rebuild-on-write semantics) wasn't justified until real usage showed brute-force scanning was a problem for the plugin's typical repo sizes.
children.bodyText:
## Alternatives considered

- **Keep Qdrant, run it out-of-process.** Rejected outright by ADR-0001
  -- reintroduces the exact operational overhead being removed.
  Remains a candidate for a future "heavy mode" storage tier, not a
  wholesale replacement.
- **An embedded vector index library (e.g. an HNSW binding) instead of
  brute-force.** Deferred rather than rejected: added complexity
  (another native binding, index-rebuild-on-write semantics) wasn't
  justified until real usage shows brute-force scanning is actually a
  problem for this plugin's typical repo sizes.

children.title: Status
children.summary: This document outlines the status of a multi-repo-isolation feature, which was accepted in 2026-09.
children.bodyText:
## Status

Accepted (multi-repo-isolation, 2026-09).

children.title: Context
children.summary: The documentation covers the context of moving from a Qdrant collection-based isolation to an SQLite-based approach in OpenCode, where plugins run against a single `worktree` per session and the same plugin installation is reused across repositories.
children.bodyText:
## Context

The original stack used one Qdrant *collection* per project as its
physical isolation boundary -- separate projects' vectors were never
comingled at the storage layer, regardless of application-level query
filtering. Moving to embedded SQLite (ADR-0002) needed an equivalent
isolation story: OpenCode plugins run against a single `worktree` per
session, but the same plugin installation is reused across every repo
a user opens with OpenCode.

children.title: Decision
children.summary: The `deriveProjectKey` function in `src/storage/project-key.ts` generates a unique project key from the session's worktree. Each project has its own SQLite file located in `~/.local/share/opencode-ai-context-plugin/projects/<key>/index.sqlite`, and there is no shared table with a `project_key` column for filtering queries.
children.bodyText:
## Decision

`src/storage/project-key.ts`'s `deriveProjectKey` derives a stable,
project-scoped key from the session's `worktree`, and each project
gets its **own SQLite file** under
`~/.local/share/opencode-ai-context-plugin/projects/<key>/index.sqlite`
(with a sibling `doc-trees.sqlite` for doc-tree data -- see ADR-0009).
There is no shared table with a `project_key` column that every query
must remember to filter by.

children.title: Consequences
children.summary:
- Isolation is structural, not query-dependent; cross-repo search requires multiple store handles.
- `src/storage/project-registry.ts` and tools for managing projects exist due to manual disk space reclaiming.
- Store file path is outside project worktree, preventing re-indexing.
children.bodyText:
## Consequences

- Isolation is structural, not query-discipline-dependent: a bug that
  forgets a `WHERE project_key = ?` clause is architecturally
  impossible here, because there is no other project's data reachable
  from an open handle to one project's file.
- Cross-repo search (an explicit, opt-in exception -- see ADR-0007's
  sibling `cross-repo-allowlist` feature) has to explicitly open
  *multiple* store handles and merge results in application code,
  rather than adding a query filter -- a deliberate trade-off: the
  common case (single-repo isolation) is free of a whole bug class, at
  the cost of cross-repo search being slightly more code.
- `src/storage/project-registry.ts` + the `ai_context_list_projects`/
  `ai_context_delete_project` tools exist because, unlike a shared
  store, deleting a project's data is now "delete a directory," which
  nothing does automatically when a repo falls out of use --
  reclaiming disk space is a manual, explicit action.
- The store's file path always lives OUTSIDE the project's own
  worktree (under the user's local data dir, not inside the repo) --
  this is also why the plugin's own writes never re-trigger its own
  `file.watcher.updated` indexing (see ADR-0012): OpenCode only watches
  the worktree, and the store file isn't in it.

children.title: Alternatives considered
children.summary: - **A single shared SQLite file with a `project_key` column on every row.** Rejected: reintroduces exactly the "every query must remember to filter" risk this decision exists to avoid, for a marginal simplicity gain (one file to manage instead of N) that doesn't matter much given SQLite files are cheap and self-contained.
children.bodyText:
## Alternatives considered

- **A single shared SQLite file with a `project_key` column on every
  row.** Rejected: reintroduces exactly the "every query must
  remember to filter" risk this decision exists to avoid, for a
  marginal simplicity gain (one file to manage instead of N) that
  doesn't matter much given SQLite files are cheap and self-contained.

The initial plan was to depend on the npm `fastembed` package, but it was found to be incompatible due to missing support for `nomic-embed-text-v1.5` and hardcoded pooling behavior. Forking `fastembed-js` to add nomic support and fix pooling was considered but rejected due to the need for maintaining a fork of someone else's abstraction.
children.bodyText:
## Context

The plugin needs an in-process embedding backend for
`nomic-ai/nomic-embed-text-v1.5` (chosen for its Matryoshka-truncatable
output and permissive license). The initial plan was to depend on the
npm `fastembed` package, since it promises exactly this: bundled ONNX
models + tokenization + pooling behind a simple `EmbeddingModel` API.

A pre-implementation audit (recorded in the session's `plan.md`,
"Auditing fastembed/nomic embedding fit") found two disqualifying
problems:

1. `fastembed`'s `EmbeddingModel` catalog **does not include nomic at
   all** -- there's no supported model identifier for
   `nomic-embed-text-v1.5`.
2. Even setting that aside, `fastembed`'s `getEmbeddings()` extraction
   is **hardcoded to the first token position (CLS pooling)**, not the
   attention-mask-weighted mean pooling `nomic-embed-text-v1.5` was
   actually trained with. Using it would silently produce degraded
   embeddings with no error -- the worst kind of failure for a
   retrieval-quality-sensitive feature.

Forking `fastembed-js` to add nomic support and fix pooling was also
considered and rejected: it would mean maintaining a fork of someone
else's abstraction for behavior that's actually quite small once
manually implemented.

children.title: Decision
children.summary: The decision involves hand-rolling an embedding pipeline that includes attention-mask-weighted mean pooling, L2 normalization, and Matryoshka dimension truncation. The pipeline is implemented in `src/embedding/embedder.ts`, with dependencies on `tokenize` and `runInference`. The REAL implementation is provided in `src/embedding/model-runtime.ts`, using `onnxruntime-node` for inference, the official `tokenizers` package for tokenization, and `@huggingface/hub`'s `downloadFileToCacheDir` for fetching the quantized ONNX export. The `createLazyEmbedder` function loads the tokenizer and ONNX session once, lazily, and shares that single loaded session between `embedQuery` and `embedDocument`. The model's ONNX graph takes `input_ids`, `token_type_ids`, and `attention_mask` as inputs and returns a single `last_hidden_state` output of shape `[1, seqLen, 768
children.bodyText:
## Decision

Hand-roll the embedding pipeline directly:

- `src/embedding/embedder.ts` implements the actual math this
  decision requires owning: attention-mask-weighted mean pooling
  (`meanPool`), L2 normalization (`l2Normalize`), and Matryoshka
  dimension truncation (`truncateMatryoshka`) -- injectable
  `tokenize`/`runInference` dependencies keep this module free of real
  I/O in unit tests.
- `src/embedding/model-runtime.ts` provides the REAL implementation of
  those two dependencies: `onnxruntime-node` for inference, the
  official `tokenizers` package for tokenization, and
  `@huggingface/hub`'s `downloadFileToCacheDir` for fetching the
  quantized ONNX export (`onnx/model_quantized.onnx`, ~137MB int8 vs.
  ~547MB fp32) and tokenizer config.
- `createLazyEmbedder` loads the tokenizer + ONNX session once, lazily
  (on first real `semantic_search`/indexing call, not at plugin
  startup), and shares that single loaded session between
  `embedQuery` and `embedDocument`.

Verified manually end-to-end (real download + real ONNX inference, not
part of the fast unit suite): the model's ONNX graph takes
`input_ids`/`token_type_ids`/`attention_mask` and returns a single
`last_hidden_state` output of shape `[1, seqLen, 768]`; L2 norm of the
resulting embedding was confirmed ≈ 1.

children.title: Consequences
children.summary:
- The plugin now directly handles pooling and normalization, avoiding abstraction mismatches.
- Int8 quantization reduces model size by 4x while maintaining negligible retrieval quality.
- Lazy loading optimizes resource usage, only loading the model when needed.
- ADR-0005 discusses the model cache location decision.
children.bodyText:
## Consequences

- No dependency on an abstraction whose model catalog and pooling
  strategy don't match this plugin's actual model -- the tradeoff is
  owning ~100 lines of pooling/normalization/truncation math directly,
  which is small and now unit-tested (`embedder.test.ts`).
- The int8-quantized model export is a deliberate quality/size
  trade-off: negligible retrieval-quality loss for a ~4x smaller
  download, matching the plugin's "no bundled heavy infra, keep it
  light" philosophy.
- Lazy loading means the first `semantic_search` call (or first
  indexing pass) in a session pays the model-load cost, not every
  OpenCode session start -- deliberate, since `semantic_search` may
  never be called in a given session.
- See ADR-0005 for the model *cache location* decision (a related but
  separate choice from the pipeline implementation itself).

children.title: Alternatives considered
children.summary: The text covers the alternatives considered for a search index, including `fastembed`, `fastembed-js`, and `@huggingface/transformers`. It mentions that `npm fastembed` was rejected due to wrong model catalog and pooling strategy, while forking `fastembed-js` was rejected due to ongoing maintenance cost. The text also considers `@huggingface/transformers` as a potential alternative, noting its completeness but smaller size and narrower dependencies.
children.bodyText:
## Alternatives considered

- **npm `fastembed` package as originally planned.** Rejected: wrong
  model catalog, wrong pooling strategy (silent quality degradation).
- **Forking `fastembed-js`.** Rejected: maintaining a fork for a
  relatively small amount of actual logic isn't worth the ongoing
  upstream-drift maintenance cost.
- **`@huggingface/transformers` (transformers.js).** Considered in the
  same audit as a heavier-but-more-complete alternative; not chosen
  because the plugin only needs a single fixed pipeline (tokenize ->
  ONNX inference -> pool -> normalize -> optionally truncate), which
  is small enough to own directly with narrower, more auditable
  dependencies (`onnxruntime-node` + `tokenizers` directly, rather than
  a larger all-in-one library).

children.title: Context
children.summary: The embedding pipeline downloads and caches a ~137MB quantized ONNX model and its tokenizer config using `@huggingface/hub`'s `downloadFileToCacheDir`. If left unset, it uses the standard shared cache location. Other plugins may also use `nomic-embed-text-v1.5` or other HF-hosted models.
children.bodyText:
## Context

The embedding pipeline (ADR-0004) needs to download and cache a ~137MB
quantized ONNX model plus its tokenizer config. The download uses
`@huggingface/hub`'s `downloadFileToCacheDir`, which accepts an
optional `cacheDir` parameter. If left unset, it uses the SAME standard
shared cache location (`$HF_HOME/hub`, `~/.cache/huggingface/hub` by
default) that Python's `huggingface_hub`/`transformers`/
`sentence-transformers` and JS's `@huggingface/transformers` all use.

The user separately runs (or may run) other OpenCode plugins that also
embed with `nomic-embed-text-v1.5` or other HF-hosted models.

children.title: Decision
children.summary: This decision removes the default `cacheDir` setting, allowing models to be downloaded into HF's shared cache unless overridden. It also maintains the `AI_CONTEXT_PLUGIN_MODEL_CACHE_DIR` option for private, fully plugin-owned caches.
children.bodyText:
## Decision

Leave `cacheDir` unset by default (`resolveModelCacheDir` returns
`undefined` unless overridden), so the download lands in HF's own
standard shared, content-addressed cache rather than a
plugin-private directory. `AI_CONTEXT_PLUGIN_MODEL_CACHE_DIR` remains
as an explicit opt-out for locked-down/air-gapped setups that want a
private, fully plugin-owned cache instead.

children.title: Consequences
children.summary:
- **Content Addressing**: Embeds with `nomic-embed-text-v1.5`, ensuring each plugin downloads the same exact blob once, reducing ~137MB downloads per plugin.
- **Model Sharing**: Deliberately different from per-project vector-store files (ADR-0003), as the model is shared, static, and non-project-specific.
- **Private Cache**: Allows users to force a private cache via `AI_CONTEXT_PLUGIN_MODEL_CACHE_DIR` on locked-down/air-gapped machines or for strict per-plugin disk isolation.
children.bodyText:
## Consequences

- If another OpenCode plugin (or any other HF-ecosystem tool on the
  same machine) also embeds with `nomic-embed-text-v1.5`, it downloads
  the exact same content-addressed blob once, and every consumer
  reuses it -- no duplicate ~137MB downloads per plugin.
- This is deliberately DIFFERENT from the per-project vector-store
  files (ADR-0003): the model is shared, static, non-project-specific
  data, so there's no isolation benefit to duplicating it the way
  per-project data must be kept separate.
- A user on a locked-down/air-gapped machine, or one who wants strict
  per-plugin disk isolation for any reason, can still force a private
  cache via `AI_CONTEXT_PLUGIN_MODEL_CACHE_DIR` without any code
  changes.

children.title: Alternatives considered
children.summary: The search index documentation discusses alternatives considered for a plugin-private cache directory, rejecting the default approach due to potential duplicate downloads across independently developed plugins using the same public model.
children.bodyText:
## Alternatives considered

- **A plugin-private cache directory by default (e.g. under
  `~/.local/share/opencode-ai-context-plugin/models/`).** Rejected as
  the default: guarantees duplicate downloads across independently
  developed plugins using the same public model, for no isolation
  benefit, since the artifact itself has no per-project or per-plugin
  sensitive content.

Framework edges are reported with an edge kind, and ambiguity is flagged with `ambiguous`. The tool's `hint` tells the agent to confirm them with the native `lsp` tool.

children.title: Context
children.summary: The search index documentation covers the `analyze_impact` feature, which was initially exposed but later removed due to its lack of a graph and the visibility of a failing tool. The key terms include `analyze_impact`, `AI_CONTEXT_PLUGIN_HEAVY_MODE`, and `not implemented yet`. The decision to remove it was based on the assumption that the graph needed heavy infrastructure, but a static graph built during indexing is now considered cheap and sufficient.
children.bodyText:
## Context

The original stack's MCP server exposed `analyze_impact`: a precomputed,
repo-wide call/import graph. Slimming the plugin first gated it behind
`AI_CONTEXT_PLUGIN_HEAVY_MODE`, then (critical-review finding
"analyze-impact-honest-stub") un-registered it, because its `execute()`
always threw "not implemented yet" -- there was no graph behind it, and a
visible tool that always fails is worse than an absent one.

Those decisions assumed the graph needed heavy infrastructure. It does
not: with tree-sitter already in the plugin (ADR-0013, ADR-0016) and an
embedded SQLite store (ADR-0002), a static graph is cheap to build during
the normal indexing pass.

children.title: Decision
children.summary: `analyze_impact` registers and uses a SQLite graph database for indexing and resolving imports and calls. It extracts symbols, imports, and calls from TypeScript/JavaScript, Python, Java, Kotlin, C#, Go, Rust, Ruby, C, and C++ files. It resolves imports to repo files and calls by name and narrows them based on same-file, imported-file, receiver, and directory evidence. It indexes files raw per update and re-resolves edges for what the batch could have changed, with graph failures not blocking chunk indexing. It extracts framework edges like React JSX components, Angular constructor/inject references, NgModule/standalone-component metadata arrays, and selector usage in inline templates. It backs up the graph to `.opencode/ai-context/backup/graph.jsonl` and flags ambiguous edges with `ambiguous`.
children.bodyText:
## Decision

`analyze_impact` is **always registered** and answers from a graph kept
in its own SQLite file (`graph.sqlite`, next to the vector store):

- **Tables** (`storage/graph-store.ts`): `graph_files`, `symbols`,
  `import_edges`, `call_edges`.
- **Extraction** (`indexing/graph/`): one tree-sitter parse per file
  yields symbols, imports and calls for TypeScript/JavaScript, Python,
  Java, Kotlin, C#, Go, Rust, Ruby, C and C++.
- **Resolution** (`import-resolver.ts`, `call-resolver.ts`): imports are
  resolved to repo files; calls are matched by name and narrowed by
  same-file, imported-file, receiver and directory evidence.
- **Indexing** (`graph-indexer.ts`, hooked into `createIndexer`): files
  are stored raw per update and edges are re-resolved once per batch,
  only for what the batch could have changed. Graph failures never block
  chunk indexing.
- **Framework edges** (`framework-extractor.ts`, TS/JS only), reported
  with an edge `kind`: React JSX component usage (`jsx`), Angular
  constructor/`@Inject`/`inject()` references (`inject`), NgModule and
  standalone-component metadata arrays (`decorator`), and selector usage
  in inline templates (`template`). `selector:` values become `selector`
  symbols on their class; a template edge keeps the raw tag in
  `qualifier` and is re-pointed at the owning class whenever selectors
  change, so the component's callers include the templates using it.
  Templates in `templateUrl` files are not analysed.
- **Backup**: `.opencode/ai-context/backup/graph.jsonl`, exported by
  `ai_context_export_backup`, restored on startup when the graph is empty.
- **Ambiguity**: edges that cannot be tied to one definition are flagged
  `ambiguous`. The tool's `hint` tells the agent to confirm them with the
  native `lsp` tool (`goToDefinition` at the call site, `findReferences`
  at the definition), with file:line locations.

`heavyMode` / `isHeavyModeEnabled()` no longer gates anything and has no
functional effect; it stays as plumbing for a future heavy-mode feature.

children.title: Consequences
children.summary: The search index documentation covers the framework's heuristic matching of JSX tags and template attributes, static name-based graph structure without type information, indexing overhead, and the continued use of the native `lsp` tool for exact results.
children.bodyText:
## Consequences

- Framework edges are heuristic: JSX tags are matched by name, and
  template attributes only when camelCase (to skip `class`, `id`, ...).
- The graph is static and name-based: no type information, no
  tsconfig `paths`, Gradle source roots, Cargo workspaces or Go module
  names in import resolution, and calls inside anonymous callbacks have no
  named caller. Precision is bounded by that; `lsp` remains the exact
  answer, and the tool says so.
- Indexing does slightly more work per file (one extra parse), and the
  graph adds one more file to the per-project data directory.
- The native `lsp` tool is still what callers should use for exact,
  type-aware results; `analyze_impact` saves round trips, it does not
  replace it.
- `.ai-context/lsp-bridge/` stays deleted: the native `lsp` tool covers
  its capability.

children.title: Alternatives considered
children.summary: The text discusses alternatives considered for a search index, including opt-in heavy mode, unregistered reliance on `lsp`, and type-aware resolution via LSP at index time.
children.bodyText:
## Alternatives considered

- **Keep it opt-in behind heavy mode.** Rejected: the graph is cheap and
  an agent benefits on any repo size.
- **Keep it unregistered and rely on `lsp` only.** Rejected: many
  sequential `lsp` queries are slow for "what does changing X affect".
- **Type-aware resolution via LSP at index time.** Rejected for now:
  needs language servers running during indexing; instead ambiguity is
  surfaced and left to the agent's on-demand `lsp` calls.

children.title: History
children.summary: The search index documentation covers the history of the `analyze_impact` feature, which was initially gated behind a plugin mode and later removed entirely.
children.bodyText:
## History

- Initial: gate `analyze_impact` behind `AI_CONTEXT_PLUGIN_HEAVY_MODE`
  (`slim-analyze-impact-drop-lspbridge`).
- Revised: un-register entirely because `execute()` was a stub
  (`analyze-impact-honest-stub`).
- Revised (this version): real implementation, always on.

children.title: Context
children.summary: The documentation covers the process of managing search index data for projects, including how to handle data outside the project's worktree and the challenges of re-indexing when starting a new clone or teammate's machine. Key terms include "search index," "ADR-0003," "local data directory," "fresh clone," "re-indexing cost," and "semantic_search/search_docs."
children.bodyText:
## Context

Per-project data (ADR-0003) lives outside the project's own worktree,
in the user's local data directory -- which means a fresh clone of a
repo (or a new teammate's machine) starts with an EMPTY index and has
to pay the full re-indexing cost (chunking + embedding every file)
before `semantic_search`/`search_docs` become useful. The
original stack's Postgres+Qdrant pair had no equivalent "ship the
index with the repo" story either -- an out-of-band export was outside
its normal operating mode.

children.title: Decision
children.summary: The `backup.ts` file exports sorted JSON Lines of the vector store and a separate file for DocTreeStore's PageIndex-style Markdown trees. It ensures commit-able and git-diffable backups inside the worktree, with a sibling file for independent diffability. On plugin startup, it auto-imports backups if the local store is empty and triggers a fresh export with `ai_context_export_backup`.
children.bodyText:
## Decision

`src/storage/backup.ts` exports the vector store as sorted JSON Lines
to `.opencode/ai-context/backup/index.jsonl` **inside the worktree**
(the opposite placement from the live per-project store) -- making it
commit-able and git-diffable (stable key order per row, sorted by
`relativePath`, so re-exporting an unchanged store produces a
byte-identical diff). A sibling `doc-trees.jsonl` in the same directory
covers `DocTreeStore`'s PageIndex-style Markdown trees (ADR-0009) the
same way, as a separate file so the two backups stay independently
diffable and a repo with no tree-indexed Markdown never gets an empty
doc-trees file created.

On plugin startup, if the current machine's local store (chunks, or
doc trees, checked independently) is empty, the corresponding backup
file is auto-imported -- never overwriting a store that already has
local data. The `ai_context_export_backup` tool triggers a fresh
export of both backups on demand, e.g. before committing.

children.title: Consequences
children.summary:
- A fresh clone or new teammate gets a working, populated index immediately after `git pull`, with no re-indexing wait.
- Both backup files are ordinary git-tracked text files, diffable and mergeable in the git sense.
- A committed backup can arrive corrupted, and `importBackup`/`importDocTreeBackup` parse and shape-validate each row independently.
- This is a manual, on-demand action, not an automatic side effect of every indexing event.
- A repo can have one backup file without the other, e.g., all code with no long-form Markdown.
children.bodyText:
## Consequences

- A fresh clone (or new teammate) gets a working, populated index
  immediately after `git pull`, with no re-indexing wait, as long as
  someone committed a reasonably fresh backup.
- Both backup files are ordinary git-tracked text files -- diffable,
  mergeable in the git sense. A committed backup can also arrive
  corrupted the same way any tracked file can (most commonly an
  unresolved git merge conflict, or a hand-edited/partially-written
  row) -- `importBackup`/`importDocTreeBackup` parse and shape-validate
  each row independently and silently skip any row that fails either
  step (a `JSON.parse` failure, a missing required field, or a
  wrong-typed field such as `vector`/`nodes` not being an array),
  rather than letting one bad line abort the entire import
  (validate-backup-import-schema, closed).
- This is an entirely manual, on-demand action (the tool), not an
  automatic side effect of every indexing event -- committing an index
  snapshot is a deliberate "share this with the team" decision, not
  background noise on every save.
- Because doc-tree and chunk backups are separate files with
  independent empty-store checks, a repo can have one without the
  other (e.g. all code, no long-form Markdown) without an artifact
  being created for the unused half.

children.title: Alternatives considered
children.summary: The text discusses two alternatives for search index backups: a single merged backup file covering both chunks and doc trees, which was rejected due to its inefficiency and potential for creating unnecessary artifacts. The other alternative is no backup at all, which was rejected as the default because it would be unacceptable for a single active developer and would impose a full re-indexing cost on every new clone/teammate/CI checkout.
children.bodyText:
## Alternatives considered

- **A single merged backup file covering both chunks and doc trees.**
  Rejected: would force every backup update to touch one file
  regardless of which half actually changed, and would create an
  artifact for doc trees even in repos with no long-form Markdown.
- **No backup at all; re-index on every fresh clone.** Rejected as the
  default: acceptable for a single active developer, but every new
  clone/teammate/CI checkout would otherwise pay the full re-indexing
  cost from zero, with no way to share that cost across a team.

description: This ADR outlines the decision to enforce both a `.gitignore` and an extension safelist at both indexing entry points in the search index. The filter is wired into both the startup full-repo walk and the `indexOneFile` function, ensuring that binaries, secrets, and vendored files are no longer read or indexed. The `shouldIndexFile` check runs before `readFile` and after `deleteChunksForFile/deleteTree`, ensuring that excluded files are correctly de-indexed.

## Status

Accepted (repo-walker-ignore-filtering, critical-review follow-up,

children.title: Context
children.summary: The documentation covers the original `.ai-context` stack's `watcher/indexer.py` and its filtering mechanisms, including the merged `pathspec` built from `.gitignore` and `config.yaml`'s `include_extensions`. The plugin's initial `repo-walker.ts` implementation lacks both filtering mechanisms, leading to potential file reading and embedding issues.
children.bodyText:
## Context

The original `.ai-context` stack's `watcher/indexer.py` combined two
filtering mechanisms before ever reading a file's content:

1. A merged `pathspec` built from the worktree's own `.gitignore` (plus
   configured extra gitignore files).
2. `config.yaml`'s `include_extensions` -- an explicit SAFELIST of
   extensions, which doubles as the binary-detection mechanism ("this
   is also what keeps binaries out -- no separate binary-detection step
   needed," per that file's own comment) rather than sniffing file
   contents.

The plugin's initial `repo-walker.ts` implementation had neither: only
a small hardcoded directory denylist (`node_modules`, `.git`, `dist`,
etc.). A critical review of the implementation flagged this as a real
gap, not a cosmetic one: without both mechanisms, every file not caught
by that small denylist -- images, archives, lockfiles, `.env`, vendored
binaries, anything a project-specific `.gitignore` excludes -- would be
read as UTF-8, chunked, embedded, and (via ADR-0007's repo-local
backup) potentially committed into git as a leaked artifact.

children.title: Decision
children.summary: The `file-filter.ts` module in `src/indexing/` implements two mechanisms: a safelist for indexing extensions and real `.gitignore` semantics using the `ignore` package. It combines these into a single predicate for the indexing pipeline and ensures both startup full-repo walks and `indexOneFile` use this filter. The `shouldIndexFile` dependency allows for incremental changes to be filtered correctly, and it runs before `readFile` and after `deleteChunksForFile`/`deleteTree`.
children.bodyText:
## Decision

`src/indexing/file-filter.ts` ports both mechanisms:

- `isIndexableExtension` -- a safelist mirroring `config.yaml`'s
  `include_extensions` (plus `INDEXABLE_FILENAMES` for the one
  extensionless entry, `Dockerfile`).
- `createIgnoreMatcher`/`loadGitignoreSync` -- real `.gitignore`
  semantics (including negation patterns like `!important.log`) via the
  `ignore` npm package, rather than hand-rolled glob matching.
- `createFileFilter` combines both into the single predicate the
  indexing pipeline needs.

Critically, this filter is wired into BOTH indexing entry points, not
just one:

1. `repo-walker.ts`'s startup full-repo walk.
2. `indexing.ts`'s `indexOneFile`, via a new optional `shouldIndexFile`
   dependency -- so `file.watcher.updated`-driven incremental changes
   (edits made during a live session) get identical filtering. Without
   this second wiring, a binary or gitignored file edited mid-session
   would bypass the startup walk's filter entirely.

The `shouldIndexFile` check runs BEFORE `readFile` in `indexOneFile`,
so a rejected file's content is never even read -- and it runs AFTER
the existing `deleteChunksForFile`/`deleteTree` calls, so a file that
becomes newly-excluded (e.g. just added to `.gitignore`) still gets its
previously-indexed chunks/tree cleaned up correctly.

children.title: Consequences
children.summary: The documentation covers the consequences of changes to the search index, including the removal of binaries, secrets, and vendored files from the committed backup, the need to remember the filter at every indexing entry point, and the correct de-indexing of newly gitignored or excluded files.
children.bodyText:
## Consequences

- Binaries, secrets (`.env`), and vendored/generated files are no
  longer read, chunked, embedded, or risked in the committed backup
  (ADR-0007).
- The filter must be remembered at every future indexing entry point --
  the two-place wiring here is not incidental; any new way of feeding
  files into the pipeline needs the same `shouldIndexFile` check.
- A file that becomes newly gitignored (or newly excluded by an
  extension change) during a live session is correctly de-indexed on
  its next `file.watcher.updated` event, not just skipped going
  forward.

children.title: Alternatives considered
children.summary: The text discusses two alternatives considered for a search index: content-sniffing binary detection and hand-rolled `.gitignore` glob matching. The first alternative was rejected due to its divergence from the original stack's approach and lack of predictability, while the second alternative was rejected because it relies on a widely used, consistent implementation and is easier to get right than hand-rolled glob matching.
children.bodyText:
## Alternatives considered

- **Content-sniffing binary detection (e.g. checking for null bytes)
  instead of an extension safelist.** Rejected: diverges from the
  original stack's proven approach, and an explicit safelist is more
  predictable/auditable than heuristic content sniffing.
- **Hand-rolled `.gitignore` glob matching.** Rejected: `.gitignore`
  semantics (negation, directory-only patterns, anchoring) are
  easy to get subtly wrong; the `ignore` npm package is a small,
  zero-dependency, widely used implementation, consistent with this
  plugin's "no bundled heavy infra, keep it light" philosophy.

description: This ADR outlines the porting of a hierarchical indexing approach for long-form Markdown documents, replacing the original chunking method. The new system uses a tree structure derived from document headings and stores it in an SQLite file, allowing for structured retrieval of content. The approach is mutually exclusive with chunking per file and avoids duplicate representations of the same content.

nodes.summary: This ADR discusses the PageIndex-style hierarchical indexing approach for long-form Markdown content, which is mutually exclusive with chunking.

children.title: Status
children.summary: This document provides a status update on the port-doc-tree-markdown project, indicating that it has been accepted and is ready for further development or deployment.
children.bodyText:
## Status

Accepted (port-doc-tree-markdown, 2026-09).

children.title: Context
children.summary: The search index documentation covers the original stack's approach to parsing long-form Markdown documents into a tree structure for navigation, inspired by the PageIndex method. It mentions decisions to treat these documents differently from source code and uses `chunker.py` to gate which files receive this treatment.
children.bodyText:
## Context

The original stack (`watcher/doc_tree_builder.py` + `mcp-server/src/
doc_tree.ts`) treated long-form Markdown (docs, ADRs, wikis) differently
from source code: instead of paragraph/semantic chunking, it parsed the
document's heading structure into a tree and let an agent navigate it
top-down (table of contents -> node summary -> full node text) --
inspired by the PageIndex approach
(https://github.com/VectifyAI/PageIndex) of reasoning-based retrieval
over a document's own hierarchical structure, rather than flat
similarity search over arbitrary-sized chunks. `chunker.py` gated which
files got this treatment vs. ordinary chunking.

children.title: Decision
children.summary: This decision splits the original search index into separate modules for parsing Markdown headings, building document trees, and searching doc trees. It also introduces a new storage mechanism for doc trees and a tool for searching them, allowing for more flexible and efficient search capabilities.
children.bodyText:
## Decision

Port this as its own path, not a chunker variant:

- `src/indexing/doc-tree-builder.ts` -- `parseMarkdownHeadings` /
  `buildDocTree` / `shouldUseTreeIndex` (the gate deciding whether a
  file is tree-indexed instead of chunked -- mutually exclusive per
  file, matching the original's gate).
- `src/storage/doc-tree-store.ts` -- persists trees in their own SQLite
  file, sibling to the vector store, same per-project directory
  (ADR-0003's isolation applies here too).
- `src/search/doc-tree-search.ts` -- ports `buildToc`/`searchDocTrees`
  (keyword-based node scoring); a `limit` on files returned replaces
  the original's `tokenBudget`, since that fed the original's
  `assembleContext` orchestrator, which this plugin never wired up (no
  equivalent orchestration layer exists here).
- `src/tools/search-docs.ts` exposes it as `search_docs`
  with three modes (`toc_only`/`summary_only`/`node_text`), letting the
  agent progressively drill down instead of getting a flat text blob.

children.title: Consequences
children.summary: The text covers the structure-aware retrieval of long-form documents, the exclusive use of tree-indexing or chunking per file, the fixed doc-tree backup gap, and future extensions for non-Markdown document formats. Key terms include tree-indexing, chunking, doc-trees.jsonl, and ADR-0007/ADR-0008.
children.bodyText:
## Consequences

- Long-form docs get structure-aware retrieval (agent can ask for just
  the TOC, then a specific node's summary, then its full text) instead
  of being chunked into arbitrary paragraph-sized pieces that lose the
  document's own organization.
- Because tree-indexing and chunking are mutually exclusive per file,
  every Markdown file is either fully tree-indexed or fully chunked --
  never both -- avoiding duplicate/conflicting representations of the
  same content.
- The doc-tree backup gap (a file separate from the chunk backup not
  covering doc trees at all) was a real critical-review finding, since
  fixed -- see ADR-0007's description of the sibling `doc-trees.jsonl`
  file.
- pandoc-based conversion of non-Markdown document formats (`.docx`
  etc.) into this same tree-indexing pipeline was discussed as a
  future extension but is NOT implemented -- today only Markdown files
  get tree-indexed; other formats are either chunked (if
  extension-safelisted, see ADR-0008) or skipped entirely.

children.title: Update (2026-10-08)
children.summary: This update removes the 8-heading threshold for tree-indexing, making all `.md` files tree-indexed without chunking. Node and document summaries are generated at index time by the `summary_llm` server, which uses the same client and failure handling as file summaries. If the `summary_llm` server is unreachable, summaries are `null`, and ranking uses titles only.
children.bodyText:
## Update (2026-10-08)

- Every `.md` file is tree-indexed; the former 8-heading threshold is gone
  (`minHeadingsForTree` now defaults to 0), so documents are never chunked.
  A file without headings becomes one root node titled with its path.
- Node and document summaries are written at index time by the `summary_llm`
  server (same client and failure handling as file summaries, own prompt).
  Without a reachable server they stay `null` and ranking uses titles only.

children.title: Alternatives considered
children.summary: The text discusses two alternatives for constructing a search index from Markdown documents: treating Markdown as a file type and using an LLM-driven tree construction method. The first alternative was rejected because it loses the document's hierarchical structure, which is valuable for structured documents. The second alternative was not adopted because it uses the document's own heading structure directly, which is sufficient for well-structured Markdown documents.
children.bodyText:
## Alternatives considered

- **Treat Markdown as just another chunkable file type.** Rejected:
  loses the document's own hierarchical structure, which is
  specifically valuable for docs/ADRs/wikis where an agent benefits
  from navigating top-down rather than getting arbitrary paragraph
  chunks ranked by similarity alone.
- **Full PageIndex-style LLM-driven tree construction (using an LLM to
  decide the tree structure, per the original PageIndex project).**
  Not adopted: the ported version uses the document's own heading
  structure directly (deterministic, no extra LLM calls needed), which
  is sufficient for well-structured Markdown docs and keeps this
  feature free of an additional LLM-call dependency.

description: This ADR discusses replacing the `SKILL.md` file with embedded workflow guidance in tool descriptions. It aims to simplify the discovery process and improve maintainability by keeping the guidance next to the tool's definition. The decision was made to embed workflow guidance directly in each tool's description string, making it visible up front and reducing the need for an extra discovery round trip.

children.title: Status
children.summary: This document outlines the status of a search index, including decisions and names mentioned.
children.bodyText:
## Status

Accepted (simplify-skill-tool-delivery, 2026-09). Partly superseded by
[ADR-0020](0020-steer-agent-to-context-tools.md): descriptions remain the
main channel, but a system-prompt hint and a bundled `index-status` skill
were added.

children.title: Context
children.summary: OpenCode's `skill` mechanism allows plugins to provide guidance in `SKILL.md` files, which are loaded via `skill({name})`. The plugin's earlier design considered delivering workflow guidance, but this feature is not currently implemented. OpenCode surfaces every registered tool's `description` field to the agent at tool-listing time, alongside built-in tools.
children.bodyText:
## Context

OpenCode has a `skill` mechanism: a plugin can ship a `SKILL.md` file
that the agent discovers and loads via a `skill({name})` call before
using the capability it describes. An earlier iteration of this
plugin's design considered delivering workflow guidance (e.g. "prefer
`grep`/`glob` for exact identifier lookups; use `semantic_search` for
conceptual/fuzzy queries instead") via a `SKILL.md`.

OpenCode already surfaces every registered tool's `description` field
to the agent at tool-listing time, alongside every built-in tool
(`grep`, `glob`, `lsp`, etc.) -- the agent sees it "for free" as part of
normal tool discovery, before ever deciding whether to call anything.

children.title: Decision
children.summary: The documentation includes workflow guidance directly within each tool's description string, providing clear instructions on when to use `grep`/`glob` instead of other methods.
children.bodyText:
## Decision

Carry the workflow guidance directly in each tool's `description`
string (e.g. `semantic_search`'s description explicitly says when to
prefer `grep`/`glob` instead), rather than via a separate `SKILL.md`
file and its associated discovery mechanism.

children.title: Consequences
children.summary:
- No extra discovery round trip: agent must decide skill relevance before guidance.
- Less indirection for maintainers: guidance next to tool definition.
- Only per-tool workflow guidance; not cross-tool orchestration.
children.bodyText:
## Consequences

- No extra discovery round trip: a `SKILL.md`-based approach requires
  the agent to have already decided the skill is relevant enough to
  invoke `skill({name})` before it can read the guidance that would
  have helped it decide that in the first place. Description-embedded
  guidance is visible up front, at the same time every other tool's
  description is.
- Less indirection for maintainers too: the guidance lives right next
  to the tool definition it applies to (`src/tools/semantic-search.ts`
  etc.), not in a separate file that has to be kept in sync with the
  tool's actual behavior.
- This only applies to per-tool workflow guidance. It does not rule out
  a `SKILL.md`/skill mechanism for something that genuinely needs
  cross-tool, multi-step workflow orchestration guidance beyond what a
  single tool's description can carry -- this plugin simply hasn't
  needed that yet.

children.title: Alternatives considered
children.summary: - **A `SKILL.md` describing when/how to use `semantic_search` vs. native tools.** Rejected for the reason above: strictly adds indirection for a single-tool workflow hint that fits naturally in the tool's own description field.
children.bodyText:
## Alternatives considered

- **A `SKILL.md` describing when/how to use `semantic_search` vs.
  native tools.** Rejected for the reason above: strictly adds
  indirection for a single-tool workflow hint that fits naturally in
  the tool's own description field.

description: This ADR discusses the decision to use OpenTelemetry API-only telemetry for the OpenCode plugin, allowing users to choose their own backend without bundling an SDK or exporter. The telemetry is dual-written, providing both an in-memory summary and standard OpenTelemetry spans with a duration histogram. This approach ensures zero-config users get the summary, and users with existing OTel infrastructure get automatic telemetry.

nodes.title: ADR-0011: OpenTelemetry API-only telemetry ("bring your own backend"), dual-written with an in-memory summary
nodes.summary: This ADR discusses the OpenTelemetry API-only telemetry approach, which involves dual-written telemetry with an in-memory summary.
nodes.bodyText: # ADR-0011: OpenTelemetry API-only telemetry ("bring your own backend"), dual-written with an in-memory summary

children.title: Status
children.summary: This document outlines the status of the search index implementation, including its acceptance and the associated components (otel-telemetry and telemetry-hooks) for the year 2026-09.
children.bodyText:
## Status

Accepted (otel-telemetry, telemetry-hooks, 2026-09).

children.title: Context
children.summary: The documentation covers the use of OpenCode's `tool.execute.before`/`tool.execute.after` plugin hooks, which fire for every tool call in a session. The key terms include telemetry, observability stack, exporter, local collector, persistence layer, and agent.
children.bodyText:
## Context

OpenCode's `tool.execute.before`/`tool.execute.after` plugin hooks fire
for EVERY tool call in a session -- native `grep`/`glob`/`lsp` calls
included, not just this plugin's own tools. That's automatic,
zero-self-instrumentation telemetry: unlike the originating monorepo's
`bench.js` CLI (external tooling, not part of this package, which
requires an agent to manually wrap/start/stop each action it wants
measured), these hooks see everything without the agent doing anything
special.

The question was what to DO with that telemetry: build/bundle a full
observability stack (an exporter, a local collector, a persistence
layer), or something lighter.

children.title: Decision
children.summary: This plugin provides telemetry for dual-write telemetry from a single recorder, exposing an in-memory summary and standard OpenTelemetry spans with a duration histogram. It uses the OTel API without bundling or managing an actual telemetry backend, allowing users to bring their own backend.
children.bodyText:
## Decision

Dual-write telemetry from a single recorder
(`src/telemetry/telemetry.ts`):

1. **An in-memory summary** -- zero-config, exposed via the
   `ai_context_telemetry_report` tool as JSON (per-tool call count, total/average
   duration, and approximate input/output token counts, using the same
   word/number/punctuation-run token approximation as `bench.js`, kept
   numerically consistent on purpose so results are comparable across
   both).
2. **Standard OpenTelemetry spans + a duration histogram**, via
   `@opentelemetry/api` -- **API only, no bundled SDK or exporter**.

Per the OTel API's own design, calling a tracer/meter with no SDK
registered is a safe no-op. That means this plugin never needs to
bundle, configure, or manage an actual telemetry backend itself --
"bring your own backend," the same pattern already used for the
LLM/embedding model backend (ADR-0004/0005: this plugin picks a
default, but doesn't force infrastructure choices on the user).

children.title: Consequences
children.summary: The documentation covers the consequences of using the `ai_context_telemetry_report` tool, including zero-config setup for users with an OTel collector, automatic collection of plugin tool-call spans and durations, and no-op behavior for users without an OTel SDK. It also mentions the generically useful telemetry surface for future benchmarking or evaluation harnesses.
children.bodyText:
## Consequences

- Zero-config users get the `ai_context_telemetry_report` tool's summary with no
  setup at all.
- Users who already run an OTel collector for their OpenCode host
  process get this plugin's tool-call spans/duration histogram
  automatically, for free, with no plugin-side configuration --
  they're using the exact same global tracer/meter providers
  `@opentelemetry/api` already exposes.
- Users with no OTel SDK configured pay effectively zero cost for the
  OTel code path (confirmed no-op by the API's own design), so there's
  no reason to feature-flag it off.
- This exposes the raw signal (spans, histogram, in-memory summary) for
  any future benchmarking or evaluation harness to consume, without this
  plugin needing to implement or own any benchmarking logic itself.
  (Benchmarking this plugin's own retrieval quality was considered and
  explicitly descoped from this project's own plan -- see `plan.md` --
  but the telemetry surface remains generically useful regardless of
  who consumes it.)

children.title: Alternatives considered
children.summary: The text discusses two alternatives for a search index: bundling a full OTel SDK + exporter or an in-memory summary only. Both alternatives were rejected due to forcing infrastructure decisions and losing the automatic zero-self-instrumentation benefit for users with existing observability infrastructure.
children.bodyText:
## Alternatives considered

- **Bundle a full OTel SDK + exporter (e.g. always export to a local
  OTLP endpoint).** Rejected: forces an infrastructure/configuration
  decision (where does telemetry go?) onto every user, even those who
  don't want it, and duplicates whatever OTel setup the user's
  OpenCode host process may already have.
- **In-memory summary only, no OTel at all.** Rejected: would lose the
  "automatic, zero-self-instrumentation" benefit for users who DO
  already have real observability infrastructure in place and would
  want this plugin's calls to show up in it.

description: This ADR discusses the decision to switch from `file.edited` to `file.watcher.updated` for re-indexing in OpenCode, aligning with the original watcher's functionality and avoiding self-triggering indexing loops.

nodes.title: ADR-0012: React to `file.watcher.updated`, not `file.edited`, for re-indexing
nodes.summary: This ADR discusses the decision to react to `file.watcher.updated` events instead of `file.edited` events for re-indexing purposes.
nodes.bodyText: # ADR-0012: React to `file.watcher.updated`, not `file.edited`, for re-indexing

children.title: Status
children.summary: The documentation covers the status of a search index, including the acceptance date and the decision to replace the watcher with hooks.
children.bodyText:
## Status

Accepted (replace-watcher-with-hooks, 2026-09).

children.title: Context
children.summary: OpenCode exposes two file-change signals: `file.edited` and `file.watcher.updated`. The Docker-based watcher replaced these, watching the filesystem directly and re-indexing on any change.
children.bodyText:
## Context

OpenCode exposes (at least) two distinct file-change signals a plugin
can subscribe to via its `event` hook: `file.edited` (fires only for
edits the agent itself made through its own tools, e.g. a `write`/`edit`
tool call) and `file.watcher.updated` (fires for changes from ANY
process -- external editors, `git pull`, another terminal, a build
step writing generated files).

The Docker-based watcher this plugin replaces (ADR-0001) watched the
filesystem directly, with no notion of "who" made a change -- it
re-indexed on any observed change, full stop.

children.title: Decision
children.summary: The documentation covers the decision to subscribe to `file.watcher.updated` instead of `file.edited` for a search index.
children.bodyText:
## Decision

Subscribe to `file.watcher.updated`, not `file.edited`.

children.title: Consequences
children.summary: The search index is designed to respond to changes made by the agent and external processes, such as user edits or `git pull`/branch switches. It does not trigger re-indexing for changes made by the plugin itself, which is handled separately.
children.bodyText:
## Consequences

- Matches what the old watcher container actually needed to catch: a
  user editing files in their own editor outside of OpenCode, a `git
  pull`/branch switch, or any other external process touching the
  worktree, all trigger re-indexing -- not just changes the agent made
  through its own tool calls.
- If `file.edited` were used instead, external changes (the common
  case of a human editing code alongside the agent) would silently
  never re-trigger indexing, leaving the index stale relative to what's
  actually on disk without the agent (or the plugin) ever being aware.
- Combined with ADR-0003's placement of the store file OUTSIDE the
  worktree, this also means the plugin's own writes (to its SQLite
  files) never re-trigger `file.watcher.updated` on themselves --
  there's no risk of a self-triggering indexing loop.

children.title: Alternatives considered
children.summary:
- **`file.edited`.** Rejected: too narrow -- would miss the exact class of external, non-agent-driven changes.
- **Both events.** Considered redundant: since `file.watcher.updated` is a superset covering everything `file.edited` would also catch (an agent's own edit is still a change on disk that the watcher observes too), listening to both would just double-fire without adding coverage.
children.bodyText:
## Alternatives considered

- **`file.edited`.** Rejected: too narrow -- would miss the exact class
  of external, non-agent-driven changes the original watcher was built
  to catch.
- **Both events.** Considered redundant: since `file.watcher.updated`
  is a superset covering everything `file.edited` would also catch (an
  agent's own edit is still a change on disk that the watcher observes
  too), listening to both would just double-fire without adding
  coverage.

nodes.title: ADR-0013: `web-tree-sitter` (WASM) grammars for per-language chunking, not native bindings
nodes.summary: This ADR discusses the creation of grammars for per-language chunking in the `web-tree-sitter` (WASM) project, focusing on not using native bindings.
nodes.bodyText: # ADR-0013: `web-tree-sitter` (WASM) grammars for per-language chunking, not native bindings

children.title: Status
children.summary: This document provides a status update for the `port-tree-sitter-chunker` follow-up, indicating that it has been accepted on 2026-09-16.
children.bodyText:
## Status

Accepted (2026-09-16), for the `port-tree-sitter-chunker` follow-up.

children.title: Context
children.summary: This documentation covers the search index implementation in `src/lib/chunker.ts`, which currently only supports paragraph-based fallback from the original stack's `watcher/chunker.py`. The remaining 1100 lines are for language-specific, tree-sitter-boundary-aware chunking for 13 languages. The plugin's install story has been focused on a single native dependency (`onnxruntime-node`), avoiding multiple language-grammar packages to reduce install-time fragility.
children.bodyText:
## Context

`src/lib/chunker.ts` currently only ports the paragraph-based fallback
from the original stack's `watcher/chunker.py`; the ~1100 remaining
lines of that file are per-language, tree-sitter-boundary-aware chunking
for ~13 languages (Kotlin, TS/TSX, JS/JSX, Python, C#, Java, Swift, Go,
Rust, Ruby, PHP, C/C++, Vue) plus dedicated Markdown/SQL/YAML handling.
Bringing that over requires a real tree-sitter dependency, and there are
two ways to get one in Node:

1. **`node-tree-sitter` + native `tree-sitter-<lang>` npm packages** --
   the reference/most mature ecosystem, but each language package is a
   native addon requiring either a prebuilt binary for the exact
   OS/arch/Node-ABI combination or a local compile toolchain
   (`node-gyp`, a C compiler, Python) at install time.
2. **`web-tree-sitter`** -- tree-sitter's official WASM binding; each
   grammar ships as a `.wasm` file loaded at runtime, no native
   compilation step anywhere in the install path.

This plugin's install story so far has been "one native dependency,
already accepted and isolated" (`onnxruntime-node`, ADR-0004) -- adding
13 more native language-grammar packages on top of that would multiply
exactly the kind of install-time fragility (per-OS/arch/Node-ABI
prebuilt-binary mismatches, CI/sandboxed-environment compile failures)
the plugin has otherwise deliberately avoided by choosing SQLite over
Postgres/Qdrant (ADR-0002) and a hand-rolled embedding pipeline over a
heavier framework (ADR-0004).

children.title: Decision
children.summary: The search index uses `web-tree-sitter` (WASM) for per-language chunking grammars, which is slower than native bindings but more reliable across platforms. WASM parsing overhead is negligible per-file but accumulates across a full initial index of large repos, so heavy mode hands very large repos to the original Docker stack. Parsing trees for a given language are only needed once a file of that language is chunked, not at plugin startup.
children.bodyText:
## Decision

Use `web-tree-sitter` (WASM) for the per-language chunking grammars, not
native `tree-sitter-<lang>` bindings.

The known cost is per-file parse overhead: WASM tree-sitter parsing is
typically ~1.2-2x slower than the native binding, which is negligible
per-file but accumulates across a full initial index of a very large
repo. This plugin already has an explicit relief valve for that case --
"heavy mode" (`AI_CONTEXT_PLUGIN_HEAVY_MODE`, ADR-0006) hands very large
repos back to the original Docker stack's brute-force-at-scale
architecture -- so accepting a modest WASM indexing-time cost for
typical repo sizes, in exchange for install reliability across
platforms/CI/sandboxes, is consistent with that existing design rather
than a new tradeoff being introduced.

Each grammar's `.wasm` file is loaded lazily per language, mirroring the
lazy-load pattern already used for the embedding model (ADR-0004) --
parse trees for a given language are only needed once a file of that
language is actually chunked, not at plugin startup.

children.title: Consequences
children.summary: The documentation covers the consequences of building a search index, including the use of `npm install` for cross-platform compatibility and the need to build grammars from source for some languages. It also mentions that the fallback behavior remains unchanged.
children.bodyText:
## Consequences

- No native compile step or prebuilt-binary matrix to maintain across
  ~13 additional language packages -- `npm install` stays reliable
  cross-platform, matching the existing `onnxruntime-node`-is-the-one-
  exception posture from ADR-0004.
- Modest per-file/aggregate parse-time cost vs. native bindings, most
  visible during a large repo's first full index -- acceptable given
  "heavy mode" already exists as the escape hatch for repos at that
  scale.
- Official prebuilt `.wasm` grammars don't exist (or aren't current)
  for every one of the ~13 target languages; a few may need building
  from source via `tree-sitter build --wasm` as part of this work,
  vendored alongside the plugin rather than fetched at runtime.
- `chunker.ts`'s existing paragraph-based `chunkText()` fallback remains
  the fallback for any language/file type without a wired-up grammar --
  this decision only changes how tree-sitter itself is obtained, not the
  fallback behavior.

children.title: Alternatives considered
children.summary:
- **`node-tree-sitter` + native per-language npm packages.** Rejected: faster and more complete grammar ecosystem, but introduces native dependency install fragility.
- **Skip tree-sitter chunking entirely, keep only the paragraph fallback.** Rejected: AST-boundary-aware chunking improves retrieval-quality-sensitive semantic search results.
children.bodyText:
## Alternatives considered

- **`node-tree-sitter` + native per-language npm packages.** Rejected:
  faster and a more complete/mature grammar ecosystem, but reintroduces
  exactly the native-dependency install fragility (per-OS/arch/Node-ABI
  prebuilt binaries or a local compile toolchain) this plugin has
  otherwise avoided; a real risk for CI and restricted/sandboxed
  environments specifically.
- **Skip tree-sitter chunking entirely, keep only the paragraph
  fallback.** Rejected: the whole point of AST-boundary-aware chunking
  (splitting on function/class boundaries rather than arbitrary
  paragraph breaks) is retrieval-quality-sensitive -- the original
  stack's `chunker.py` exists precisely because paragraph-only chunking
  produces worse `semantic_search` results for source code.

children.title: Status
children.summary: This document outlines the status of a search index feature, including its acceptance date and changes made to the configuration file.
children.bodyText:
## Status

Accepted (config-file feature, user-directed, 2026-09-16). Amended by [ADR-0029](0029-opt-in-enabled-flag-and-default-template.md): the generated file now carries every default as an active value, an `enabled` master switch (off by default) and no secrets; the separate example file was removed.

children.title: Context
children.summary: The documentation covers the process of configuring a search index with four settings, each configurable via environment variables. It explains that these settings are inherently machine/session-local and cannot be shared across contributors without each contributor exporting the same environment variable. The user requested a project-level config file that would read an `ai-context.config.yaml` file and use it as a middle tier between environment variables and built-in defaults, allowing for overrides if the environment variable is set.
children.bodyText:
## Context

By the time this decision was made, four settings existed, each
configurable ONLY via an `AI_CONTEXT_PLUGIN_*` environment variable:
`AI_CONTEXT_PLUGIN_DATA_DIR` (project-key.ts), `AI_CONTEXT_PLUGIN_EMBED_DIMS`
and `AI_CONTEXT_PLUGIN_MODEL_CACHE_DIR` (model-runtime.ts), and
`AI_CONTEXT_PLUGIN_HEAVY_MODE` (heavy-mode.ts). Env vars are inherently
machine/session-local -- there was no way for a team to commit a shared
default (e.g. "this monorepo always wants `embed_dims: 256`") without
every contributor separately exporting the same env var themselves.

The user asked for a project-level config file, explicitly requesting:
"a full config file loader which read a ai-context.config.yaml... env
vars become overrides on top of the file" -- i.e. env var still wins if
set, but the file becomes the new middle tier between env var and
built-in default.

children.title: Decision
children.summary: This decision outlines how the search index is configured using a YAML file, with specific settings for data directory, model cache directory, embedding dimensions, and heavy mode. The configuration file is placed in the `.opencode/` directory alongside other metadata files, and its precedence is determined by explicit options, environment variables, and built-in defaults. Each setting has a final fallback parameter in consuming modules, and the YAML keys are mapped to camelCase fields for TypeScript. The decision ensures fault tolerance by logging errors and degrading gracefully when configuration files are malformed or missing.
children.bodyText:
## Decision

- One YAML file per project: `.opencode/ai-context.config.yaml`, resolved
  via `resolveConfigFilePath(worktree)`. Placed inside `.opencode/`
  alongside this plugin's other worktree-local, team-shareable metadata
  (the repo-local backup and the cross-repo allow-list, see ADR-0007 and
  the allow-list's own module) -- NOT alongside the live SQLite store,
  which ADR-0003 deliberately keeps OUTSIDE the worktree.
- Precedence, applied per-setting rather than centrally: explicit
  function option (only relevant to this plugin's own tests) > env var
  (if explicitly set) > this config file > built-in default. Each
  consuming module (`resolveDataDir`, `resolveModelCacheDir`,
  `resolveOutputDims`, `isHeavyModeEnabled`) takes the config-file value
  as an additional, final-fallback parameter rather than the config file
  being centrally merged into `process.env` or similar -- keeps each
  setting's precedence contract visible and independently unit-testable
  at its own module, matching this codebase's existing per-module
  resolve-function style.
- YAML keys are snake_case (`data_dir`, `model_cache_dir`, `embed_dims`,
  `heavy_mode`) to match the file's own idiom, mapped to camelCase
  `AiContextConfigFile` fields for the TS side.
- Scope is exactly these 4 existing settings -- no new, previously
  un-configurable internals (e.g. the chunker's `maxLines`) were promoted
  to configurable as part of this change, to keep the increment bounded.
- Fault tolerance mirrors `backup.ts`'s per-row validation: a missing
  file, an empty file, malformed YAML, a non-mapping top level, or a
  wrong-typed known key are all `console.error`-logged and degrade to
  "no override from this key/file" -- never thrown. One bad line in a
  committed config file must not break the whole plugin for every
  contributor who pulls it.

children.title: Consequences
children.summary:
- The documentation covers changes to commit settings, doc comments for `heavy-mode.ts`, behavior of `resolveOutputDims`, and adds `yaml` as a dependency.
- Key terms include `embed_dims`, `heavy-mode.ts`, `resolveOutputDims`, and `yaml`.
children.bodyText:
## Consequences

- A team can now commit `embed_dims: 256` (say, for a very large
  monorepo) once, and every contributor gets it automatically, while
  still being able to locally override via an env var for one-off
  debugging without editing the committed file.
- `heavy-mode.ts`'s doc comment previously argued heavy mode is "not a
  repo config file setting... a machine/session performance trade-off,
  not a team convention to version-control" -- this is explicitly
  superseded: it's now also settable via the config file (a team CAN
  commit a shared default), with the env var still available as a
  per-machine override on top, matching the other 3 settings' identical
  treatment. Keeping heavy mode's precedence inconsistent with the other
  3 settings would have been a confusing, unjustified special case.
- `resolveOutputDims`'s existing "env var set but invalid falls straight
  to `undefined`" behavior was deliberately widened to "falls through to
  the config-file value instead" -- a backward-compatible expansion,
  since existing callers that never pass a config-file value see
  identical behavior to before.
- Adds `yaml` as a direct dependency (was already present transitively
  via `@opencode-ai/plugin` -> `effect`; pinned directly for stability/
  clarity rather than relying on the transitive resolution holding).

children.title: Alternatives considered
children.summary:
- **JSON instead of YAML.** Rejected: no comments support, and this file is exactly the kind of "explain what each knob does, right next to it" document that benefits from inline comments (see the generated `.opencode/ai-context.config.yaml`).
- **A single central "load all config" function that mutates `process.env` or a shared config object.** Rejected: would hide each setting's precedence contract behind one large function instead of keeping it visible (and independently unit-testable) at each consuming module, breaking from this codebase's existing `resolveDataDir`/`resolveModelCacheDir`/`resolveOutputDims` per-module pattern.
- **Config file overrides win over env vars.** Rejected per the user's explicit direction ("env vars become overrides on top of the file")--env vars stay the higher-precedence, machine-local escape hatch.
