description: This ADR outlines the decision to bundle a TypeScript plugin into a single file and install it globally in OpenCode's plugin directory. The plugin is built using esbuild, with runtime dependencies marked as external and resolved from `node_modules`. The installation script copies the bundle to the global plugin directory and updates the shared config directory's `package.json` to preserve dependencies. This approach allows contributors to install the plugin with a single command, ensuring consistency and avoiding reinstallation across multiple repositories.

children.title: Status
children.summary: This documentation covers the status of a search index, including its packaging and setup processes, user-directed actions, and the date it was accepted.
children.bodyText:
## Status

Accepted (packaging/setup, user-directed, 2026-09-16).

children.title: Context
children.summary: OpenCode loads local plugins directly from a plugin directory, either `.opencode/plugins/` or `~/.config/opencode/plugins/`. The package is a multi-module TypeScript project with `node_modules` dependencies, some of which ship native addons. Local plugins requiring external packages must have a `package.json` in OpenCode's config directory, which OpenCode runs `bun install` against at startup.
children.bodyText:
## Context

OpenCode loads **local plugins** directly from a plugin directory --
either `.opencode/plugins/` (project-level) or
`~/.config/opencode/plugins/` (global) -- with no build/install step of
its own: whatever JS/TS file is in that directory is loaded as-is at
startup. This package, however, is developed as a normal multi-module
TypeScript project (`src/hook/`, `src/storage/`, `src/embedding/`, etc.)
with `node_modules` dependencies, some of which ship native addons
(`better-sqlite3`, `onnxruntime-node`, `tokenizers`).

Two related questions needed answers: (1) how does a multi-file TS
source tree become the single file layout OpenCode's local-plugin
loader expects, and (2) where do a local plugin's native npm
dependencies get resolved from, since OpenCode does not run `npm
install`/`bun install` against the plugin directory itself.

Per OpenCode's own docs (https://opencode.ai/docs/plugins/#dependencies):
local plugins needing external packages must have a `package.json`
placed in OpenCode's own **config directory** (`~/.config/opencode/`),
against which OpenCode runs `bun install` at startup, caching the result
in `~/.cache/opencode/node_modules/`.

children.title: Decision
children.summary: This plugin bundles its TypeScript code into a single JavaScript file, installs it globally in the OpenCode plugins directory, and uses Mise to manage its dependencies.
children.bodyText:
## Decision

- **Bundle, don't ship source.** `scripts/build.mjs` (esbuild) bundles
  `src/index.ts` into one file, `dist/accso-ai-context.js` (ESM,
  `node18` target, with a sourcemap). This plugin's OWN `src/` modules
  are inlined; native/non-inlinable runtime dependencies
  (`better-sqlite3`, `onnxruntime-node`, `tokenizers`,
  `@huggingface/hub`, `ignore`, `@opentelemetry/api`) are marked
  `external` and stay as plain `import` statements resolved from
  `node_modules` at runtime, same as any normal npm consumer would
  resolve them. `yaml` is deliberately NOT external -- it's pure JS with
  no native addon, so esbuild inlines it like this plugin's own code.
- **Install to the GLOBAL plugin directory** (`~/.config/opencode/
  plugins/accso-ai-context.js`), not the project-level one. This plugin
  is meant to be usable across every repo a contributor works in (see
  ADR-0002's per-project SQLite isolation, which already makes one
  globally-installed plugin instance safe to reuse across many
  worktrees/sessions) -- a project-level install would mean
  re-installing into every single repo instead of once per machine.
- **`scripts/install-plugin.sh`** copies the bundle to the global plugin
  directory, then merges (not overwrites) this plugin's runtime
  dependency versions into `~/.config/opencode/package.json`, so a
  second, unrelated plugin's own dependencies already listed there (or
  added later by that plugin's own setup script) are preserved rather
  than clobbered. OpenCode's own `bun install` at its next startup then
  resolves them -- this script does not run `bun`/`npm install` itself.
- **`accso-ai-context` as the file/tool-family name** (user-directed) --
  distinct from the working directory's own name
  (`opencode-ai-context-plugin`), matching what will be a different,
  more product-facing name once extracted to its own repository.
- **`mise.toml` + `mise run setup`** wraps `install-plugin.sh` (via a
  `depends: [build]` task chain) as the one-command entry point, and
  separately pins the dev/build/test Node toolchain version -- see the
  file's own header comment for why it's fully self-contained and
  doesn't merge with (or depend on) the parent `ai-context` monorepo's
  own `mise.toml`.

children.title: Consequences
children.summary:
- Provides a global install script for OpenCode plugins without needing to understand local dependency resolution.
- Ensures idempotent reinstallation of the plugin, only updating its own dependencies in the shared config.
- Maintains manual synchronization between esbuild config and bash script for `EXTERNAL_RUNTIME_DEPS` to avoid conflicts.
- Copies sourcemaps alongside the bundle and ignores the `dist/` directory as a build artifact.
children.bodyText:
## Consequences

- A contributor (or, eventually, an end user once this is a published
  package) runs one command (`mise run setup`, or `npm run build &&
  ./scripts/install-plugin.sh` without mise) and gets a working global
  install, without needing to understand OpenCode's local-plugin
  dependency-resolution mechanism themselves.
- Re-running the install script after a rebuild is safe and idempotent:
  it always overwrites `accso-ai-context.js` itself (that's the point of
  reinstalling a new build) but only adds/updates this plugin's OWN
  dependency entries in the shared config-directory `package.json`,
  never removing or overwriting unrelated entries another plugin may
  have added.
- `scripts/build.mjs`'s `EXTERNAL_RUNTIME_DEPS` list and
  `install-plugin.sh`'s own copy of that list must be kept in sync
  manually (both files carry a comment saying so) -- a genuine, accepted
  maintenance cost of not sharing a single source of truth between an
  esbuild config and a bash script; revisit if this drifts in practice.
- Sourcemap (`accso-ai-context.js.map`) is copied alongside the bundle
  for stack traces during local debugging; `dist/` itself is
  gitignored -- it's a build artifact, not source.

children.title: Alternatives considered
children.summary: This documentation covers the alternatives considered for a search index, including publishing to npm, using OpenCode's plugin config-file mechanism, project-level install, and shipping `src/` unbundled with relative imports.
children.bodyText:
## Alternatives considered

- **Publish to npm, use OpenCode's `plugin: [...]` config-file
  mechanism instead of a local file.** Rejected for now: this package
  isn't published yet (still living inside the parent monorepo, per
  this repo's own README) -- worth revisiting once it's extracted and
  versioned independently; nothing about the bundling step itself needs
  to change if that happens later.
- **Project-level install (`.opencode/plugins/`).** Rejected: would
  require every repo a contributor works in to separately receive the
  bundle/config, instead of once per machine -- see the isolation
  argument above for why one global install is already safe.
- **Ship `src/` unbundled and rely on OpenCode/Bun resolving relative
  imports directly.** Rejected: OpenCode's local-plugin loader expects
  a single loadable file per plugin, not a package directory with its
  own `node_modules`/multi-file module graph.

children.title: Status
children.summary: This document outlines the status of a search index, noting that it has been accepted and is a refinement of ADR-0013 regarding the use of WASM over native bindings.
children.bodyText:
## Status

Accepted (2026-10). Refines ADR-0013 (WASM over native bindings stays).

children.title: Context
children.summary: `tree-sitter-wasms` 0.1.13 bundles grammars built with tree-sitter CLI, including versions for C#, Java, Kotlin, Python, and TypeScript/JavaScript. It pins `web-tree-sitter` to 0.20.8, which produces ERROR nodes that are not suitable for symbol/import/call-graph extraction and blast-radius analysis.
children.bodyText:
## Context

`tree-sitter-wasms` 0.1.13 bundles grammars built with tree-sitter CLI
0.20 from old grammar versions (C# 0.20, Java 0.20, Kotlin 0.3,
Python 0.21, TypeScript/JavaScript 0.20) and pinned `web-tree-sitter` to
0.20.8. Modern syntax (C# 12+, Java 21, Python 3.12, TS 5.x, Kotlin 2.x)
produced ERROR nodes -- unacceptable for the symbol/import/call-graph
extraction that blast-radius analysis needs.

children.title: Decision
children.summary: The documentation covers the decision to use `web-tree-sitter` ^0.27 and its prebuilt `.wasm` grammars for languages like C#, Java, Python, TypeScript (including TSX), JavaScript, Kotlin, Go, Rust, Ruby, C, and C++. The parser-loader maps grammar names to `.wasm` files and resolves them with `createRequire`. The test ensures modern syntax for each language without errors.
children.bodyText:
## Decision

- Depend on `web-tree-sitter` ^0.27 and the upstream grammar packages
  (`tree-sitter-c-sharp`, `-java`, `-python`, `-typescript` (also TSX),
  `-javascript`, `@tree-sitter-grammars/tree-sitter-kotlin`), each of
  which ships a prebuilt `.wasm`. No grammar is built from source.
- Also load `tree-sitter-go`, `-rust`, `-ruby`, `-c` and `-cpp` the same
  way, so the symbol/import/call graph can cover those languages too.
  They are parser-loader entries only; chunking for them stays on the
  regex tier until graph extraction needs more.
- `parser-loader.ts` maps grammar names to `<package>/<file>.wasm` and
  resolves them with `createRequire`; `web-tree-sitter` is an esbuild
  external (it loads its own runtime `.wasm` from `node_modules`).
- `test/unit/grammar-modern-syntax.test.ts` guards each language with
  current-version syntax and asserts no ERROR nodes.

children.title: Consequences
children.summary: The text discusses the consequences of changes to the search index, including the removal of certain grammars and the requirement for grammar packages to be installed alongside the bundle. It also mentions that the Grammar ABI must remain compatible with the runtime, which is currently version 14/15 and supported by version 0.27.
children.bodyText:
## Consequences

- Grammars track their languages; the unused `tree-sitter-wasms` grammars
  PHP and Swift are gone from the loader (Go, Rust, Ruby, C and C++
  are back via their upstream packages). Adding a
  language now means adding its upstream package + one map entry.
- Grammar packages must be installed next to the bundle (same as the
  other externals; see `scripts/install-plugin.sh`).
- Grammar ABI must stay compatible with the runtime (currently 14/15,
  supported by 0.27).

The decision avoids building native addons for storage and ensures consistent behavior across different runtimes.

children.title: Status
children.summary: The documentation covers the status of a search index, indicating it is accepted as of October 2026.
children.bodyText:
## Status

Accepted (2026-10).

children.title: Context
children.summary: The documentation covers the decision to use `better-sqlite3` as the embedded store for OpenCode, which runs on Bun. It explains that `better-sqlite3` was not in `trustedDependencies`, leading to its native addon not being built and Bun 1.3.14 panicking when trying to load a missing addon at plugin start, causing the OpenCode/ACP process to fail.
children.bodyText:
## Context

ADR-0002 chose `better-sqlite3` as the embedded store. OpenCode runs on
Bun, and Bun only runs a package's install script when the package is in
`trustedDependencies`. `better-sqlite3` was not, so its native addon was
never built, and Bun 1.3.14 does not throw when asked to load a missing
addon: it panics (`NAPI FATAL ERROR`, exit code 133) and takes the whole
OpenCode/ACP process down at plugin start.

children.title: Decision
children.summary: The documentation covers the decision to use a SQLite database adapter for three stores, which is implemented in `src/storage/sqlite.ts`. The adapter uses `exec`, `prepare`, `run/get/all`, `pragma`, and `transaction` methods. Under Bun, it uses the built-in `bun:sqlite`. Under Node, it uses `better-sqlite3`, which is required lazily to avoid loading it when Bun is used. The `install-plugin.sh` script no longer installs `better-sqlite3`.
children.bodyText:
## Decision

All three stores open their database through `src/storage/sqlite.ts`, a
thin adapter over the few calls they use (`exec`, `prepare`
`run/get/all`, `pragma`, `transaction`, `close`). Under Bun it uses the
built-in `bun:sqlite` (nothing to install or build); under Node (unit
tests, tooling) it uses `better-sqlite3`, required lazily so Bun never
tries to load it. `install-plugin.sh` no longer installs `better-sqlite3`.

children.title: Consequences
children.summary: The documentation covers the changes made to the search index, including the removal of native addons for storage and plugin start dependencies, the use of two SQLite implementations with different behavior, and the continued use of native addons for `onnxruntime-node` and `tokenizers`.
children.bodyText:
## Consequences

- No native addon to build for storage; plugin start no longer depends on
  install scripts or prebuilt binaries.
- Two SQLite implementations behind one adapter: a behavior difference
  between them would only show up in one runtime (the adapter normalises
  the known one, `get()` returning `null` vs `undefined`).
- `onnxruntime-node` and `tokenizers` are still native addons; they are
  only loaded when the embedder is first used.

children.title: Alternatives considered
children.summary: The text discusses two alternatives for a search index: adding `better-sqlite3` to `trustedDependencies` and using `bun:sqlite`. Both alternatives were rejected due to issues with compiler or network prebuild downloads and failed builds crashing the process.
children.bodyText:
## Alternatives considered

- **Add `better-sqlite3` to `trustedDependencies`.** Rejected: needs a
  compiler or a network prebuild download on every machine, and a failed
  build still ends in a process crash rather than an error.
- **`bun:sqlite` only.** Rejected: the unit tests and tooling run on Node.

description: This ADR outlines a solution to improve indexing progress reporting for JetBrains AI Assistant (ACP) by creating an in-memory progress tracker and mirroring it to a status file. The status file is written atomically with throttling, and the agent provides feedback in chat. The solution ensures that users can follow indexing progress and handle failures gracefully without hiding the rest of the repository from search.

children.title: Status
children.summary: The documentation covers the status of a search index, indicating it is accepted as of October 2026.
children.bodyText:
## Status

Accepted (2026-10).

children.title: Context
children.summary: The search index documentation covers the process of indexing files in a repository, including the time it takes and the issues encountered when running under JetBrains AI Assistant (ACP). Key terms include indexing, repository, CPU, RAM, fan noise, progress report, client app log, and unreadable file.
children.bodyText:
## Context

The first index of a repository embeds every file and runs for minutes.
Under JetBrains AI Assistant (ACP) the user saw nothing but CPU, RAM and
fan noise: the indexer reported no progress, and the channels that could
carry it are dead ends over ACP (`docs/observability.md`: TUI toasts and
injected chat messages never reach the client; `client.app.log` only lands
in opencode's log file). A failing file also aborted the whole batch, so
one unreadable file silently left the rest of a batch unindexed.

children.title: Decision
children.summary: The documentation covers the in-memory progress tracker, status file mirroring, indexing status retrieval, indexing notices, file indexing failures, and directory exclusion. Key terms include `index-progress`, `status-file`, `indexingNotice`, `file-filter`, and `file.watcher.updated`.
children.bodyText:
## Decision

- An in-memory progress tracker (`src/indexing/index-progress.ts`) is the
  single source of truth: phase, done/total, rate/ETA, and the files whose
  indexing failed.
- It is mirrored to `.opencode/ai-context/index-status.json`
  (`src/indexing/status-file.ts`): atomic write (tmp file + rename),
  throttled to one write per 2 s, except phase changes and newly failed
  files, which are written immediately. The file stays after the run
  (`phase: "done"`) so the last result remains inspectable.
- `index_status` returns the same data in an `indexing` block,
  including the status file path.
- `semantic_search`, `search_docs` and `analyze_impact` attach
  an `indexingNotice` while a run is active, so the agent tells the user
  that a missing hit may only mean "not indexed yet". Array results are
  wrapped as `{ indexingNotice, results }` only in that case.
- A file that fails to index is skipped and recorded (error, attempt
  count). The next watcher event for it, or the next startup pass, retries
  it; a success removes the entry, another failure increments `attempts`.
- `.opencode/ai-context/` is never indexed (`file-filter.ts`), otherwise
  every status write would come back as `file.watcher.updated`.

children.title: Consequences
children.summary: The documentation covers the consequences of indexing a search engine, including how to monitor progress with a command and the status file's location and management. It also mentions that two plugin instances write to the same file, which is harmless, and that failures are only held in memory and re-attempted on restart.
children.bodyText:
## Consequences

- Users can follow indexing with `while true; do clear; cat .opencode/ai-context/index-status.json; sleep 1; done`
  from any frontend, and the agent can relay progress in chat.
- The status file lives in the worktree and changes constantly. Add
  `.opencode/ai-context/index-status.json` to the project's `.gitignore`
  (the backup in the same directory is meant to be committed, this file
  is not). The plugin cannot enforce that.
- Two plugin instances (opencode bootstraps plugins twice) write the same
  file; the last write wins, which is harmless for a progress mirror.
- Failures are only held in memory for the current process; a restart
  re-attempts every file anyway.
- `semantic_search` output changes shape (array -> object) while indexing.

children.title: Alternatives considered
children.summary: The documentation covers alternatives considered for a search index, including TUI toasts, OS notifications, status files, and aborting on error.
children.bodyText:
## Alternatives considered

- **TUI toasts / injected chat messages / `permission.ask`.** Rejected:
  confirmed not to reach ACP clients.
- **OS notifications for progress.** Rejected for per-step progress (too
  noisy); still an option for start/finish.
- **Status file under `data_dir` (outside the worktree).** Rejected: the
  user wants an easily accessible file, and excluding the directory in the
  filter removes the feedback-loop risk.
- **Aborting the batch on error (previous behavior).** Rejected: one bad
  file must not hide the rest of the repository from search.

description: This ADR discusses optimizing search indexing to prevent memory issues by limiting token count and using a soft guard mechanism.

nodes.title: ADR-0019: Bounded memory during indexing
nodes.summary: This ADR discusses the implementation of a bounded memory strategy during the indexing process to prevent excessive memory usage. Key terms include bounded memory, indexing process, and memory management strategies.
nodes.bodyText:
# ADR-0019: Bounded memory during indexing

Status: accepted

children.title: Context
children.summary: The text covers indexing a repository that caused the opencode host process to use 16-31 GB of RSS and fill the swap. The key terms are indexing, opencode host process, RSS (Resident Set Size), swap, ONNXruntime memory growth, token count, chunker, and search(). The decision is to use two plugin bootstraps per session indexed in parallel, the ORT arena keeps the peak, and `search()` loads every vector per query.
children.bodyText:
## Context

Indexing a repository drove the opencode host process to 16-31 GB RSS and
filled the swap. Measured cause: onnxruntime memory grows quadratically with
the token count of one input (512 tokens ~0.5 GB, 4096 ~4.5 GB), while the
chunker bounded only lines, so a single 15 000-character chunk was enough.
Contributing: two plugin bootstraps per session indexed in parallel, the ORT
arena kept the peak, and `search()` loaded every vector per query.

children.title: Decision
children.summary: The documentation covers the decision-making process for a search index, including token embedding settings, chunk splitting, runtime optimization, memory management, and notification mechanisms.
children.bodyText:
## Decision

- Embedder caps tokens (`embed_max_tokens`, default 512); chunks are split to
  fit (`chunk-splitter.ts`); files over `max_file_bytes` are skipped.
- ORT session: no CPU arena/mem pattern, sequential execution, `embed_threads`.
- One shared runtime per worktree (`runtime-registry.ts`): one tracker, one
  model session, one startup pass, serial batches.
- Soft guard (`memory-guard.ts`, `max_memory_mb`, default 4096): GC + wait,
  then abort the run as `failed` with a readable reason.
- `search()` reads the table in rowid pages and keeps only the top-K.
- Native OS notifications for start/finish/failure (`os_notifications`).

children.title: Consequences
children.summary:
- Hard RSS cap is best effort, token cap is actual bound.
- Long chunks split, retrieval granularity changes.
- Skipped files visible in `index-status.json`, retried on change.
children.bodyText:
## Consequences

- A hard RSS cap is impossible inside a Bun process; the guard is best effort,
  the token cap is the actual bound.
- Very long chunks are split, so retrieval granularity changes slightly.
- Skipped files are visible in `index-status.json` and retried on change.

description: This ADR outlines changes to the search index to steer the agent towards context tools, improving efficiency and relevance. Key decisions include rewriting tool descriptions, appending a system prompt rule, adding a new `repo_structure` tool, and tracking context-tool usage with telemetry.

nodes.title: ADR-0020: Steer the agent to the context tools
nodes.summary: This ADR discusses steering the agent to use context tools, providing guidance on how to implement this feature. Key terms include "context tools," "steering the agent," and "ADR-0020."
nodes.bodyText:
# ADR-0020: Steer the agent to the context tools

Status: accepted

children.title: Context
children.summary: The documentation covers the use of grep/glob/read tools and their preference over a plugin's tools. It also mentions that skills are loaded on demand only, making them the weakest lever.
children.bodyText:
## Context

The agent preferred opencode's built-in grep/glob/read over this plugin's
tools. The `semantic_search` description even said "Prefer grep/glob first".
Skills are loaded on demand only, so they are the weakest lever.

children.title: Decision
children.summary:
- **Rewrite tool descriptions**: `semantic_search` for concept questions, `grep/glob` for exact identifiers.
- **Experimental chat system transform**: Appends a rule block to the system prompt, disabling `agent_hint`.
- **New tool `repo_structure`**: Directory tree with file count and languages, cross-repo allowlist.
- **AI context telemetry report**: Measures context-tool calls vs grep/glob, overall and per session.
- **No separate `list_recent_changes` tool**: `index_status` provides recent changes.
children.bodyText:
## Decision

- Rewrite tool descriptions: `semantic_search` is used first for concept
  questions; grep/glob only for exact identifiers.
- Append a short rule block to the system prompt via the
  `experimental.chat.system.transform` hook (runs server-side, also under
  ACP). Config `agent_hint: false` disables it.
- New tool `repo_structure`: directory tree from the index (dirs first with
  file count and languages), `dir_path`, `depth`, and `project` to inspect
  another allowed project (cross-repo allowlist). Structure only, no
  summaries, so no extra model or RAM.
- `ai_context_telemetry_report` gets `view: "adoption"`: share of context-tool calls
  vs grep/glob, overall and per session, to measure whether steering works.
- No separate `list_recent_changes` tool: `index_status` already
  returns the most recently indexed files.

children.title: Consequences
children.summary:
- The hook is experimental in opencode; if inactive, only descriptions apply.
- The hint costs a few hundred tokens per request.
- Cross-project reads open the other project's SQLite store; `repo_structure` reads only file paths, not vectors.
children.bodyText:
## Consequences

- The hook is marked experimental in opencode; if inactive, only the
  descriptions apply.
- The hint costs a few hundred tokens per request.
- Cross-project reads open the other project's SQLite store; `repo_structure`
  reads only file paths, not vectors.

children.title: Alternatives considered
children.summary: The text discusses two alternatives for a search index: one that loads skills on demand and is rarely triggered, and another that appends nudges to broad grep results, which are deferred until adoption numbers indicate their need.
children.bodyText:
## Alternatives considered

- Skill only: loaded on demand, rarely triggered.
- Nudge appended to broad grep results (`tool.execute.after`): deferred until
  the adoption numbers show it is needed.

children.title: Amendment: admin tools
children.summary: The documentation for admin tools includes descriptions and phrases that map user requests to specific tool names, such as `ai_context_export_backup`, `ai_context_export_index_tree`, and `ai_context_delete_project`. The descriptions also mention the trigger for each tool, such as "which files are indexed" and "delete project." Without these lines, the agent would not match user requests to the appropriate tools.
children.bodyText:
## Amendment: admin tools

The hint and the descriptions of the admin tools now also carry the phrases a
user says: "create an ai context backup" maps to `ai_context_export_backup`,
"which files are indexed" to `ai_context_export_index_tree`, and the
descriptions of the project list, telemetry report and delete tools name their
trigger. `ai_context_delete_project` tells the agent to confirm with the user
first. Without these lines the agent never matched such requests to a tool.

description: This ADR outlines the decision to move the embedding model loading process from each opencode instance to a separate background worker process. The worker runs in a Unix socket and is started on demand by the first plugin instance, sharing the model with all others. The worker exits after 10 minutes without clients or when its RSS exceeds a specified limit, with clients reconnecting and respawning. If the worker cannot start, clients fall back to in-process embedding with a problem report.

nodes.title: ADR-0021: Shared embedding worker outside opencode
nodes.summary: This ADR discusses the decision to move the shared embedding worker outside of the opencode directory.
nodes.bodyText:
# ADR-0021: Shared embedding worker outside opencode

Status: accepted

children.title: Context
children.summary: The text discusses issues with loading ONNX models inside host processes, leading to memory growth and crashes. It mentions that several instances duplicated the model, causing performance issues and potential system failures.
children.bodyText:
## Context

Every opencode instance (and every ACP session) loaded its own ONNX model
inside the host process. The model session, its memory arena and quadratic
attention peaks made the host grow to GBs, and a memory kill (exit 137)
took the whole opencode down. Several instances also duplicated the model.

children.title: Decision
children.summary: The search index uses a background process to run an embedding model, which communicates with clients via a unix socket. The worker script is installed next to the opencode plugins and runs in a Bun environment with specific settings. It exits after 10 minutes without clients or when its memory usage exceeds a limit, and clients reconnect and respawn after a retry. If the worker cannot start, clients fall back to in-process embedding with a problem report.
children.bodyText:
## Decision

- The embedding model runs in ONE background process per user, started on
  demand by the first plugin instance and shared by all others.
- Transport: newline-delimited JSON over a unix socket
  (`<data dir>/embed-worker.sock`, or `$TMPDIR` if the path would exceed the
  socket path limit). The worker is the arbiter: a second worker finding a
  live socket exits, a stale socket file is replaced.
- The worker script `ai-context-worker.mjs` is installed next to (not in)
  `~/.config/opencode/plugins/`, since opencode loads every file there as a
  plugin. It resolves native deps from `~/.config/opencode/node_modules`.
- It is started with the host binary and `BUN_BE_BUN=1` (opencode is a
  compiled Bun; the variable makes it run a script like `bun`; verified with
  opencode 1.18.34). Plain node/bun ignore the variable.
- Lifecycle: exits after 10 min without clients, or after a request once its
  RSS exceeds `max_memory_mb`; clients then reconnect and respawn (one retry).
  Inference runs one request at a time across all clients.
- If the worker cannot start, the client falls back to in-process embedding
  (with a problem report). `shared_worker: false` or
  `AI_CONTEXT_SHARED_WORKER=0` disables it.
- Log: `<data dir>/embed-worker.log`.

children.title: Consequences
children.summary: The text covers the consequences of running a search index with an AI context worker. It mentions that the host size remains small, and the first instance's embedding settings win for the worker's lifetime. The plugin requires `ai-context-worker.mjs` to be installed and must exit reliably to ensure proper cleanup.
children.bodyText:
## Consequences

- The host stays small; a runaway model only costs the worker.
- The first instance's embedding settings (threads, max tokens, model cache,
  dims) win for the worker's lifetime.
- Needs `ai-context-worker.mjs` installed (`scripts/install-plugin.sh`);
  without it the plugin embeds in-process as before.
- A detached process must exit reliably; idle exit and SIGTERM cleanup cover
  this.

children.title: Alternatives considered
children.summary: The text discusses two alternatives considered for indexing: moving indexing into the worker and requiring `node`/`bun` on PATH.
children.bodyText:
## Alternatives considered

- Moving indexing (not only embedding) into the worker: larger change, the
  SQLite writes are cheap; may follow.
- Requiring `node`/`bun` on PATH: not guaranteed for ACP users.

description: This ADR proposes moving the indexer into a shared worker to reduce per-instance memory usage and improve indexing performance. The worker will handle indexing tasks for multiple projects concurrently, with each project having its own queue to prevent conflicts. The plugin will send indexing requests and receive progress updates, while the worker manages Tree-sitter parsers, chunking, graph extraction, and SQLite writes. The decision includes changes to the indexing protocol, worker interface, and fallback mechanism.

nodes.title: ADR-0022: Move the indexer into the shared worker
nodes.summary: This ADR discusses the proposal to move the indexer into a shared worker, which aims to improve performance and scalability by allowing multiple requests to share resources. Key terms include shared worker, indexer, performance optimization, and scalability.
nodes.bodyText:
# ADR-0022: Move the indexer into the shared worker

Status: proposed (plan only, not implemented)

children.title: Context
children.summary: The documentation covers the process of moving the embedding model out of opencode, which affects indexing operations that run inside each opencode instance. Key terms include embedding model, directory walk, file reads, Tree-sitter WASM parsing, chunking, graph extraction, SQLite writes, per-process guard (`runtime-registry.ts`), and indexing instances.
children.bodyText:
## Context

ADR-0021 moved the embedding model out of opencode. The rest of indexing
still runs inside every opencode instance: directory walk, file reads,
Tree-sitter WASM parsing, chunking, graph extraction and the SQLite writes.
That costs CPU and memory per instance and needs a per-process guard
(`runtime-registry.ts`) so the two bootstraps of one session do not index
in parallel. Two instances on the same worktree still run two indexers.

children.title: Decision (proposed)
children.summary: The search index plugin indexes worktrees and paths, using Tree-sitter parsers and SQLite files. It manages indexing queues per worktree, progress events, memory guards, and fallbacks. The worker receives config per request and handles indexing in-process if the worker is unreachable.
children.bodyText:
## Decision (proposed)

The worker also indexes. The plugin sends `index { worktree, paths | "all" }`
and gets progress events back; the worker owns Tree-sitter parsers, chunker,
graph extraction and the writes to the project's SQLite files.

- One indexing queue per worktree in the worker, so concurrent instances
  never index the same project twice and never hit `database is locked`.
- Progress events feed the existing tracker and `index-status.json`
  (ADR-0018); the plugin keeps the status file and OS notifications.
- Memory guard and `max_memory_mb` apply to the worker; opencode stays small.
- Search, tools and hooks stay in the plugin (read-only on the stores,
  WAL allows readers during writes).
- The worker needs config per request (exclude patterns, `max_file_bytes`,
  chunk limits), sent with each `index` call rather than fixed at spawn.
- Fallback stays: if the worker is unreachable, index in-process as today.

children.title: Phases
children.summary: The documentation covers the phases of a search index, including protocol messages, worker-side queue, and interface changes for creating an indexer. It also mentions measuring RSS and CPU usage before and after.
children.bodyText:
## Phases

1. Protocol: `index`/`progress`/`done`/`failed` messages, worker-side queue
   per worktree (tests with a fake indexer, like `worker.test.ts`).
2. Move `createIndexer` + walker + graph indexer behind an interface the
   worker implements; plugin calls it through the client.
3. Wire progress into the tracker; keep in-process fallback.
4. Measure RSS and CPU per instance before and after.

children.title: Consequences
children.summary: The search index documentation covers the consequences of using a single indexer per project, worker stability, and bundling Tree-sitter WASM and grammars into the worker bundle.
children.bodyText:
## Consequences

- Lower per-instance memory and a single indexer per project.
- The worker becomes a larger piece to keep stable; a crash interrupts
  indexing (the existing delta reconciliation resumes it).
- Bundling Tree-sitter WASM and grammars into the worker bundle must be
  checked (they are external packages resolved from the config dir).

children.title: Alternatives considered
children.summary: The text discusses two alternatives for indexing: keeping it in-process and one worker per project.
children.bodyText:
## Alternatives considered

- Keep indexing in-process and only bound it further: simpler, but each
  instance still pays the parser and file-content memory.
- One worker per project: more processes, no gain over one queue per project.

description: This ADR outlines a new naming scheme and description rules for search index tools, ensuring consistency and clarity in tool usage. It specifies that research tools should have no prefix, while admin tools should use `ai_context_`. The ADR includes a test to enforce the scheme and provides descriptions for each tool, detailing what it covers, what it does not, when to use it, and the next step.

nodes.title: ADR-0023: Tool naming scheme and description rules
nodes.summary: This ADR outlines the naming conventions and description rules for tools in the search index.
nodes.bodyText:
# ADR-0023: Tool naming scheme and description rules

Status: accepted

children.title: Context
children.summary: The documentation covers the search index and its tools, explaining inconsistencies in naming and roles. It mentions `search_docs` and `index_status` with the `ai_context_` prefix, while `telemetry_report` lacks a prefix. The tool `semantic_search` incorrectly claims to cover code and docs, but Markdown docs are not searchable through it.
children.bodyText:
## Context

Tool names mixed two styles by build order, not by role: `search_docs` and
`index_status` carried the `ai_context_` prefix although agents use them for
research, while `telemetry_report` (admin) had none. `semantic_search` also
claimed to cover "code and docs", but Markdown docs are tree-indexed and not
searchable through it, so agents searched docs with the wrong tool.

children.title: Decision
children.summary: - **Decision**: The documentation covers search index tools, including `semantic_search`, `repo_structure`, `analyze_impact`, `search_docs`, and `index_status`. It also mentions admin tools prefixed with `ai_context_`. The test enforces a scheme. Descriptions state the tool's purpose, code vs docs differences, use cases, return values, and next steps (`read` with line range). `index_status` indicates indexing triggers: empty or partial results, or an `indexingNotice`.
children.bodyText:
## Decision

- **Research tools** (used by the agent while working), no prefix:
  `semantic_search`, `repo_structure`, `analyze_impact`, `search_docs`,
  `index_status`.
- **Admin tools**, prefix `ai_context_`: `ai_context_list_projects`,
  `ai_context_delete_project`, `ai_context_export_backup`,
  `ai_context_allow_repo`, `ai_context_telemetry_report`.
- A test enforces the scheme.
- Descriptions state: what it covers and what it does NOT (code vs docs),
  when to use it, what it returns, and the next step (`read` with the line
  range). `index_status` states its trigger: empty or partial results, or an
  `indexingNotice`.

children.title: Consequences
children.summary: This documentation describes changes in the search index, renaming several keys and removing aliases. It also mentions that unprefixed names could potentially conflict with future built-in tools, but the five specific names are considered unique enough to accept this risk.
children.bodyText:
## Consequences

- Renamed: `ai_context_search_docs` -> `search_docs`,
  `ai_context_index_status` -> `index_status`,
  `telemetry_report` -> `ai_context_telemetry_report`. No aliases are kept.
  Prompts or skills that use the old names must be updated.
- Unprefixed names could collide with future built-in opencode tools; the
  five names are specific enough to accept that risk.

description: This ADR outlines a roadmap for improving retrieval quality in a search index without using vector databases, symbol lookups, or deterministic summaries. The plan includes a baseline benchmark, replacing keyword boosts with FTS5 BM25 and reciprocal rank fusion, embedding context with path and symbol names, creating a `find_symbol` tool for symbol lookup, generating deterministic file summaries from AST/graphs, and using ANN indexes for search above 20-30k chunks.

nodes.title: ADR-0024: Retrieval quality roadmap (no vector DB, symbol lookup, deterministic summaries)
nodes.summary: This ADR outlines a roadmap for improving retrieval quality in search indexes, focusing on non-vector databases, symbol lookups, and deterministic summaries.
nodes.bodyText: # ADR-0024: Retrieval quality roadmap (no vector DB, symbol lookup, deterministic summaries)

children.title: Status
children.summary: The documentation covers the status of a search index implementation, including features like FTS5 BM25 + RRF, cross-encoder reranker, path/symbol embedding prefix, `find_symbol`, file summaries, and experimental LLM support. It also mentions the status of a baseline benchmark and ANN index.
children.bodyText:
## Status

Accepted (2026-10-06). Implemented: FTS5 BM25 + RRF, cross-encoder reranker,
path/symbol embed prefix, `find_symbol`, file summaries (deterministic, optional
OpenAI-compatible LLM) and best-effort enabling of the native `lsp` tool
(`OPENCODE_EXPERIMENTAL_LSP_TOOL`, only effective if the host reads flags after
plugin load). Not done: baseline benchmark, ANN index.

children.title: Context
children.summary: The documentation covers the search index implementation, including vector databases for faster search and routing without Docker. It discusses the use of brute-force cosine similarity and an ANN index for improved search speed, while routing is handled by the calling agent. The original stack's L1 summaries are from an LLM server, and `resolve_symbol` is provided by opencode's native `lsp` tool.
children.bodyText:
## Context

Open questions: is a vector DB needed for better search, and how do we cover
the original stack's L1 summaries, routing and `resolve_symbol` without Docker?

- Brute-force cosine is exact; an ANN index only makes search faster, not
  better (and slightly lossy). Measured: ~110 ms at 2k, ~580 ms at 10k,
  ~1.75 s at 30k chunks.
- Routing: the original stack already removed its routing LLM; the calling
  agent drives retrieval.
- L1 summaries in the original come from an LLM server (LM Studio).
- `resolve_symbol` in the original is LSP definition/references/hover, which
  opencode's native `lsp` tool provides.

children.title: Decision (plan, in order)
children.summary: The documentation covers a search index decision plan, including baseline benchmarks, ranking changes, embedding context, symbol lookup tools, deterministic file summaries, and ANN indices.
children.bodyText:
## Decision (plan, in order)

1. **Baseline benchmark** on two indexed projects (fixed query set, recall@k),
   before changing ranking.
2. **FTS5 BM25 + reciprocal rank fusion** replacing the keyword boost; then a
   small ONNX **cross-encoder reranker** in the shared worker.
3. **Embed context**: prefix chunk text with path and symbol name.
4. **`find_symbol` tool** on the existing symbol index (name/prefix to file,
   line, kind, signature); keep the native `lsp` tool for compiler-grade
   answers and mention it in the agent hint. Verify the `lsp` tool is enabled
   in the installed opencode version first.
5. **Deterministic file summaries** from AST/graph (exports, signatures, doc
   comments, imports), embedded as a file-level vector. An LLM-generated
   variant stays optional and opt-in.
6. **ANN index** (e.g. hnswlib/usearch, inside the worker) only above roughly
   20-30k chunks per project; before that, `embed_dims` truncation and a
   vector cache in the worker.

Each step is test-first and gated by the benchmark from step 1.

children.title: Consequences
children.summary: The documentation covers the consequences of not using a vector database, Docker, or an LLM server. It also mentions that the lookup tool is lighter and the `lsp` tool covers the rest, and quality gains are measured rather than assumed.
children.bodyText:
## Consequences

- No vector database, no Docker, no LLM server required.
- No ported `resolve_symbol`; the lookup tool is lighter and the `lsp` tool
  covers the rest.
- Quality gains are measured, not assumed.

description: This ADR outlines a solution to improve search indexing performance by resuming indexing processes, managing cross-process index leases, and handling stale files. It introduces fingerprints for indexed files, removes indexed files that are no longer present, and uses a lease system to manage concurrent indexing processes.

nodes.title: ADR-0025: Resumable indexing and cross-process index lease
nodes.summary: This ADR discusses the design of a resumable indexing system and the use of cross-process index leases to manage concurrent indexing processes. It covers topics such as indexing strategies, lease management, and error handling in a distributed search environment. Key terms include resumable indexing, cross-process index lease, and distributed search architecture.
nodes.bodyText: # ADR-0025: Resumable indexing and cross-process index lease

children.title: Status
children.summary: The documentation covers the status of a search index, noting it as accepted on 2026-10-06.
children.bodyText:
## Status

Accepted (2026-10-06).

children.title: Context
children.summary: The documentation covers the process of running ACP sessions, which involves re-embedding every file into SQLite files without change detection. It mentions the duplicated CPU/RAM, lock contention, and inability to continue where a previous run stopped due to the in-process guard not spanning processes.
children.bodyText:
## Context

Every ACP session is its own opencode process. Each ran the startup pass and
re-embedded **every** file (no change detection), all writing to the same
SQLite files: duplicated CPU/RAM, lock contention, and no way to continue where
a previous run stopped. The in-process guard (ADR-0021 runtime registry) does
not span processes.

children.title: Decision
children.summary: The search index documentation covers the process of indexing files, including fingerprinting, stale file removal, and lease management. Key terms include fingerprint, vector store, file_state table, EMBED_FORMAT_VERSION, index.lock, and heartbeat.
children.bodyText:
## Decision

1. **Fingerprints:** after a file is fully indexed, the vector store records
   `size:mtime` (`file_state` table). Files whose fingerprint matches (and that
   have chunks) are skipped, so a restart, a second session or an interrupted
   run continues with the remaining files. Failed files have no fingerprint and
   are retried. A changed `EMBED_FORMAT_VERSION` clears fingerprints with the chunks.
2. **Stale files:** the startup pass removes indexed files that are gone from the
   walk (deleted or newly excluded).
3. **Lease:** `index.lock` next to the project database (`pid` + heartbeat every
   10 s). Indexing batches run while holding it; another process waits (polls
   every 3 s) and then only finds the unfinished files. A lease of a dead
   process or without heartbeat for 45 s is taken over.

children.title: Consequences
children.summary: This documentation covers the consequences of indexing processes in a search index, including single indexing per project, fast subsequent sessions, a waiting process with phase `scanning`, and the need for a first pass re-indexing when restoring backups. It also mentions that older plugin versions do not honor the lease.
children.bodyText:
## Consequences

- One indexing process per project at a time; later sessions are fast.
- A waiting process shows phase `scanning` and may overwrite
  `index-status.json` until it gets the lease.
- Restored backups carry no fingerprints, so the first pass re-indexes once.
- Processes running an older plugin version do not honour the lease.

description: This ADR outlines changes to cross-repository tools and parallel indexing in the search index. It introduces a `project` key for research tools, allows them to access other projects' stores, and optimizes indexing by parallelizing file embedding and LLM requests.

nodes.title: ADR-0026: Cross-repo tools and parallel indexing
nodes.summary: This ADR discusses the development of cross-repository tools and parallel indexing for a search index. Key terms include cross-repo tools, parallel indexing, and search index.
nodes.bodyText: # ADR-0026: Cross-repo tools and parallel indexing

children.title: Status
children.summary: The documentation covers the status of a search index, noting it as accepted on 2026-10-06.
children.bodyText:
## Status

Accepted (2026-10-06).

children.title: Context
children.summary: The documentation covers the functionality and limitations of the search index, including how different modules can access other projects and the slow indexing process due to single-threaded processing and blocking calls.
children.bodyText:
## Context

1. Only `semantic_search` and `repo_structure` could look into other allowed
   projects; `find_symbol`, `analyze_impact` and `search_docs` were limited to
   the current repo, and a repo added with `ai_context_allow_repo` took effect
   only after a restart (the allowlist was read once at startup).
2. Indexing was slow: the shared worker ran one inference at a time, the
   indexer handled one file at a time, and the file-summary LLM call blocked
   the embedding of the same file.

children.title: Decision
children.summary: The documentation covers the decision-making process for cross-repository indexing, including how tools handle projects, skills, and parallel indexing settings.
children.bodyText:
## Decision

1. **Cross-repo:** all research tools accept an optional `project` key (from
   `ai_context_list_projects`). `find_symbol` and `analyze_impact` use the
   other project's `graph.sqlite`, `search_docs` its `doc-trees.sqlite`. Unknown
   or not allowed keys return an error listing the allowed ones. A graph/doc
   file that does not exist is never created in the other project's folder.
   `ai_context_allow_repo` opens the stores immediately.
2. **Skill:** the bundled `cross-repo` skill describes the sequence
   `ai_context_list_projects` → `ai_context_allow_repo` → tool with `project`.
3. **Parallel indexing:** `embed_concurrency` (default 3) sets both the number
   of files indexed in parallel (`fileConcurrency`) and the inference slots of
   the worker (`concurrency`, default 1 when unset). The summary LLM request is
   started before the file's chunks are embedded and awaited afterwards.
   Defaults raised to `embed_threads: 6`, `max_memory_mb: 6144`.

children.title: Consequences
children.summary:
- Faster indexing at the cost of CPU and transient RAM; `embed_consent: 1` restores sequential behaviour.
- Paths in cross-repo results are relative to the other repo; `read` only works inside the current project.
- The same file appearing twice in one batch could be indexed concurrently; startup batches contain each file once, so this is accepted.
- Not measured yet: real speed-up on a fresh index (see `docs/status.md`).
children.bodyText:
## Consequences

- Faster indexing at the cost of CPU and transient RAM; `embed_concurrency: 1`
  restores sequential behaviour.
- Paths in cross-repo results are relative to the other repo; `read` only works
  inside the current project.
- The same file appearing twice in one batch could be indexed concurrently;
  startup batches contain each file once, so this is accepted.
- Not measured yet: real speed-up on a fresh index (see `docs/status.md`).

## Status

Accepted (2026-10-08).

children.title: Context
children.summary: The startup pass skips files with unchanged `size:mtime` fingerprints, affecting how files are indexed and causing issues with document trees and tree-indexed documents.
children.bodyText:
## Context

The startup pass skips a file whose `size:mtime` fingerprint is unchanged. That
made changes to *how* files are indexed invisible: documents chunked by an
older version stayed chunks, doc trees without summaries (LLM offline) stayed
empty, and tree-indexed documents were re-read on every start because the skip
test required code chunks. Trees of deleted documents were never removed,
since the stale-file scan only looked at chunks.

children.title: Decision
children.summary: The documentation covers the decision-making process for a search index, including how fingerprints are stored with version suffixes, how unchanged files are skipped, the stale-file scan process, fallback summaries for code files, forced re-indexing options, and file visibility reporting.
children.bodyText:
## Decision

- The stored fingerprint carries a representation suffix: `#doc<DOC_INDEX_VERSION>`
  for tree-indexed document types; for code `#code<N>` only when
  `CODE_INDEX_VERSION > 1`, and `#nosum` while file summaries are off. Switching
  summaries on, or bumping a version, re-indexes only the affected file kind;
  stores written before this ADR stay valid for code. `EMBED_FORMAT_VERSION`
  remains the full-store reset.
- An unchanged file is skipped only if its index is healthy: code needs chunks;
  a document needs a tree and no chunks (documents are trees only), and a tree
  without any summary is rebuilt while a summarizer is configured (cheap: no
  embedding; the LLM is skipped after three failures).
- The stale-file scan includes doc-tree paths (`DocTreeStore.listPaths`).
- Fallback summaries (amendment, 2026-10-12): when `summary_llm` is configured
  but a code file's summary had to be the deterministic text, the fingerprint
  gets a `detsum` flag (`<fp>#detsum`, or `+detsum` after other suffixes). On a
  later start with an LLM configured, a flagged file gets only its summary chunk
  rewritten (reason `summaries`, no re-embedding of the other chunks); the flag
  is dropped when the LLM answered, kept otherwise. Without a configured LLM the
  flag is ignored.
- Forced re-index (amendment, 2026-10-12): the config keys `reindex_chunks` and
  `reindex_summaries` make the next startup pass ignore fingerprints (reason
  `upgrade`). Chunks only: files are re-chunked and re-embedded, the stored
  summary chunk is kept. Summaries only: just the summary chunk is rewritten
  (documents are rebuilt as a whole, their summaries live in the tree). Both:
  full re-index. After a run without failed files or abort the plugin sets the
  flags back to `false` by editing only those lines of the config file; an
  incomplete run keeps them on so it is repeated.

- Visibility: the indexer classifies every file before the run
  (`new`, `changed`, `removed`, `upgrade` = new index format, `repair`,
  `summaries`) and reports only files that need work. Up-to-date files are
  not counted, so a normal start no longer announces "Indexing started: N
  files". `index-status.json` carries `reasons` (counts per reason). Healing
  (`upgrade`/`repair`/`summaries`) pops up even for a few files: "Updating
  index: 42 files (40 new index format, 2 repaired)" and "Index update
  finished"; plain new/changed runs keep the old popups and the 20-file
  threshold.

children.title: Consequences
children.summary: The documentation covers the consequences of various search index settings and changes, including how flagged files are handled, document re-indexing behavior, and the impact of server downtime on parsing. Key terms include flagged files, re-indexing, server downtime, and version constants.
children.bodyText:
## Consequences

- A flagged file is retried on every start while the LLM stays down (one cheap
  attempt, no re-embedding).
- Upgrading re-indexes documents once; code files are untouched.
- When the summary server is permanently down, documents are re-parsed on each
  start (three quick failed calls, then none).
- Changing the chunker or doc-tree builder now requires bumping the matching
  version constant in `src/indexing/indexing.ts`.

children.title: Context
children.summary: The text covers the backup of a search index using an `index.jsonl` file with vectors as JSON float arrays. The backup is 63 MB for 3,711 chunks, with each vector being approximately 17 KB. The text mentions that Git cannot delta-compress float noise, leading to bloated history when changes are made.
children.bodyText:
## Context

The chunk backup was one `index.jsonl` with vectors as JSON float arrays: 63 MB
for 3,711 chunks (17 KB per vector), close to GitHub's 100 MB push limit and
growing with the repo. Git cannot delta-compress float noise, so every changed
copy also bloated history.

children.title: Decision
children.summary: The search index uses base64 float16 vectors for storage, with a precision loss below 1e-3 relative. Rows are distributed into shards based on a stable FNV-1a hash of the file path, with a maximum shard size of 10 MiB. The index is exported by deleting legacy files and stale shards, and imported by reading the legacy file and all shards. Doc-tree and graph backups remain unchanged.
children.bodyText:
## Decision

- Vectors are stored as base64 float16 (`vector16`, 2 bytes per dimension,
  about 2 KB instead of 17 KB). Precision loss is below 1e-3 relative; export
  after import is byte-stable because the values are already half precision.
- Rows go to `index-NNNN.jsonl` shards chosen by a stable FNV-1a hash of the
  file path, `maxShardBytes` (default 10 MiB) bounds the target size. The shard
  count is a power of two estimated from chunk count and average row size, so
  it changes rarely, a file's chunks stay together and a change rewrites one
  shard. Rows stay sorted by id inside a shard.
- Export deletes the legacy `index.jsonl` and stale shards first. Import reads
  the legacy file (float arrays) and all shards; per-row validation and
  skipping of broken rows is unchanged. Doc-tree and graph backups are small
  and unchanged.

children.title: Consequences
children.summary: The search index shrinks from 63 MB to 10.8 MB with two shards, old committed backups remain importable, and restored vectors differ by half-precision rounding. Beyond 50k chunks, int8 vectors can be used with a new row key for further optimization.
children.bodyText:
## Consequences

- The measured backup shrinks from 63 MB to 10.8 MB (two shards).
- Old committed backups stay importable; the next export migrates them.
- Restored vectors differ from the originals by half-precision rounding; with
  brute-force cosine search this is negligible, but a benchmark would confirm.
- Beyond roughly 50k chunks a further 2x is possible with int8 vectors behind
  a new row key; not needed yet.

children.title: Context
children.summary: The plugin indexes repositories, including those with low interest, and generates a config file with comments. Users need to read documentation to understand the settings effectively.
children.bodyText:
## Context

The plugin started indexing every repository opencode was opened in, including
ones where nobody wanted it (cost: CPU, RAM, a model download, files written into
`.opencode/`). The generated config file listed every key only as a comment, so
users still had to read the documentation to learn the effective settings.

children.title: Decision
children.summary: The documentation covers the `enabled` key in `.opencode/ai-context.config.yaml`, which is opt-in and controls whether the AI Context plugin is active. It also mentions the `api_key_env` environment variable for the summarizer, which is used to read the API key from the environment.
children.bodyText:
## Decision

- New top-level key `enabled` in `.opencode/ai-context.config.yaml`. It is
  **opt-in**: absent, `false` or unparsable (malformed file, wrong type) means
  off. `AI_CONTEXT_PLUGIN_ENABLED` (`1`/`true`, `0`/`false`) overrides the file in
  both directions (precedence as in ADR-0014).
- Off means: the plugin returns no hooks. The config file is still created when
  missing, but nothing else happens: no index or doc-tree store, no startup or
  watcher indexing, no worker, no tools, no agent hint, no bundled skills, no
  `.opencode/.gitignore`, no popups. The gate sits right after the config is
  loaded in `createAiContextHooks`.
- The generated file starts with `enabled: false` and then lists every setting
  with its **actual built-in default** as an active value. Machine-specific
  (`data_dir`, `model_cache_dir`, `embed_dims`) and optional (`exclude`,
  `heavy_mode`) keys stay commented. `config-template.test.ts` asserts that the
  template parses to exactly the code's default constants, so the two cannot
  drift apart.
- Existing config files are never rewritten. A file without `enabled` therefore
  switches the plugin off after the upgrade (strict opt-in, chosen on purpose);
  this repository's own file got `enabled: true`.

- Secrets stay out of the committed file (amendment, 2026-10-12): `summary_llm`
  takes no literal `api_key` (ignored with a warning); the key is read from the
  environment variable named by `api_key_env` (default
  `AI_CONTEXT_SUMMARY_LLM_API_KEY`), and the built-in default key `omlx` is gone.
  On HTTP 401 the summarizer raises `SummaryLlmAuthError` ("API key not set" or
  "rejected", with the `export ...` command); the plugin shows it as an OS popup
  and as a `notices` entry in `index-status.json` / `index_status`, cleared when
  the next run starts. Summaries fall back to the deterministic text as before.

children.title: Consequences
children.summary: This documentation covers the consequences of enabling and configuring the AI Context plugin for a search index. Key terms include `AI_CONTEXT_SUMMARY_LLM_API_KEY`, `enabled: true`, `summary_llm`, and `AI_CONTEXT_PLUGIN_ENABLED`.
children.bodyText:
## Consequences

- Setups that relied on the default key `omlx` must export
  `AI_CONTEXT_SUMMARY_LLM_API_KEY=omlx` once.
- Breaking for existing users: add `enabled: true` once per repository (or set
  the environment variable).
- Defaults copied into a user's file no longer follow later changes of the
  built-in defaults; users who never edit a line keep the old value.
- `summary_llm` is active in the template, so after enabling, file content goes
  to the local default server (`127.0.0.1:8000`), exactly as before; `summary_llm:
  false` turns it off.
- Tests that exercise the plugin set `AI_CONTEXT_PLUGIN_ENABLED=1` at the top of
  the test file; disabled-behaviour tests unset it explicitly.

children.title: Amendment: index tree and error log files
children.summary: The `index-tree.md` file lists indexed files with export date, repository, branch, and commit. The `error.log.md` file collects reported problems, failed files, and failed runs. Both are git-ignored and written only when the plugin is enabled.
children.bodyText:
## Amendment: index tree and error log files

Two generated files join `index-status.json` in `.opencode/ai-context/`:
`index-tree.md` (tool `ai_context_export_index_tree`, refreshed after each
completed indexing run) lists the indexed files with export date, repository,
branch and commit; `error.log.md` collects every reported problem, failed file
and failed run, size-capped. Both are git-ignored and written only when the
plugin is enabled (entries recorded before the enabled gate are buffered and
dropped if the plugin stays off), so a disabled plugin still only creates the
config file.

children.title: Alternatives considered
children.summary: The text discusses two alternatives for handling plugins in search indexes: a default-on option with a kill switch and rewriting existing configuration files to add missing keys.
children.bodyText:
## Alternatives considered

- Default-on with an `enabled: false` kill switch: keeps upgrades non-breaking
  but leaves the plugin running in repositories that never asked for it.
- Rewriting existing config files to add missing keys: would edit user files and
  discard their formatting.

# Architecture Decision Records

This folder records the significant, hard-to-reverse decisions made while
building `opencode-ai-context-plugin` -- the *why*, not just the *what*.
Each ADR is a snapshot of the reasoning at the time it was written; if a
later decision supersedes one, the older ADR is marked `Superseded by
ADR-00NN` rather than deleted or rewritten, so the history of *why we
changed our minds* stays intact.

This package is being developed inside the `ai-context` monorepo but is
written and documented as a standalone, independently extractable
project (see the root `README.md` and `NOTICE`) -- these ADRs are
self-contained and don't assume familiarity with the parent repo,
though several explicitly contrast a decision against what
`.ai-context/`'s older Docker-based stack used to do, since that's the
system this plugin replaces.

nodes.bodyText:
# Architecture

The plugin runs **inside the opencode host process** (Bun, also under ACP in
the JetBrains AI Assistant). The memory-heavy embedding model runs in one
**shared worker process** per user. Everything else is local files.

children.title: Components
children.summary: The documentation covers the components of an OpenCode search index, including hooks/plugins, indexer, search, observability, embedding worker, and storage. Key terms include hook/plugin.ts, indexer, search, observability, embedding worker, and storage.
children.bodyText:
## Components ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph Host["opencode host (one per session/ACP instance)"] Hooks["hook/plugin.ts
tools + event + system hook"] Idx["Indexer
chunk · graph · doc-tree"] Search["Search
vector · keyword · doc-tree · graph"] Obs["Observability
status file · OS notify · OTel"] end subgraph Worker["shared embedding worker (1 per user)"] ORT["onnxruntime-node
nomic-embed-text-v1.5"] end subgraph Store["~/.local/share/opencode-ai-context-plugin/projects/<key>"] V[("index.sqlite
chunks + vectors")] D[("doc trees")] G[("symbol/import/call graph")] end WT[".opencode/ai-context/
status · backup · allowlist"] Hooks --> Idx --> V & D & G Hooks --> Search --> V & D & G Idx -- "embed (unix socket, NDJSON)" --> ORT Search -- "embedQuery" --> ORT Idx --> Obs --> WT Hooks -. backup .-> WT ```

children.title: Indexing pipeline
children.summary: The indexing pipeline processes files, skipping unchanged ones and purging removed or excluded files. It uses Markdown and tree-eligible files for doc-tree building, chunking for non-Markdown files, and extracts symbols, imports, and calls. Delta indexing skips unchanged files and purges removed or excluded files, with failures noted instead of aborting the run.
children.bodyText:
## Indexing pipeline ```mermaid flowchart TD A["startup reconciliation walk
or file.watcher.updated (debounced)"] --> B{"file filter
.gitignore · extensions · exclude · max_file_bytes"} B -- skip --> X["status file: skipped"] B -- ok --> C{"Markdown and tree-eligible?"} C -- yes --> T["doc-tree builder → doc-tree store"] C -- no --> D["chunker chain
tree-sitter → regex → data-format → paragraph"] D --> E["decorator fix · dispatch sub-chunking · token-budget split"] E --> F["embedDocument (worker)"] F --> G["vector store (delta upsert)"] B -- ok --> H["graph extractor → symbols, imports, calls"] G & T & H --> P["progress → status file, OS notices, memory guard"] ``` Delta indexing: unchanged files are skipped, removed or newly excluded files are purged. Failures are skipped with a note (file, error, attempts) instead of aborting the run.

children.title: Query flow
children.summary: The query flow involves an agent sending a semantic search request to a plugin tool, which embeds the query and sends it to an embedding worker. The worker returns a vector, which is then used to perform a cosine search on SQLite stores for live and allowlisted projects. The results are merged, sliced, and keyword boosted before being returned to the agent. If indexingNotice is true, the agent reads files at a specified line range.
children.bodyText:
## Query flow

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant Ag as Agent
  participant Pl as Plugin tool
  participant W as Embedding worker
  participant S as SQLite stores
  Ag->>Pl: semantic_search(query)
  Pl->>W: embedQuery
  W-->>Pl: vector
  Pl->>S: cosine search (paged), own + allowlisted projects (live, no restart)
  S-->>Pl: candidates
  Pl->>Pl: keyword boost (0.25), merge, slice
  Pl-->>Ag: chunks + indexingNotice?
  Ag->>Ag: read file at line range
```

children.title: Process model
children.summary: The process model describes how the embedding worker is started and managed. It uses a unix socket for communication between instances, with stale sockets replaced. Inference is serial across clients, and the first instance's settings apply for the worker's lifetime. The worker runs using opencode binary or node/bun, and moving the indexer to the worker is proposed.
children.bodyText:
## Process model ```mermaid flowchart LR I1["opencode acp #1"] & I2["opencode acp #2"] & I3["opencode acp #3"] -- socket --> W["embedding worker
~0.4-0.55 GB"] W -. "idle 10 min or RSS limit → exit" .-> E((exit)) I1 -. "worker unavailable → in-process fallback" .-> I1 ``` The worker is started on demand by whichever instance needs it first, checked via a unix socket; a stale socket is replaced. Inference is serial across clients. The first instance's settings apply for the worker's lifetime ([ADR-0021](adr/0021-shared-embedding-worker.md)). The worker runs through `BUN_BE_BUN=1` using the opencode binary, or `node`/`bun` when available. The indexer itself still runs in the host; moving it is proposed in [ADR-0022](adr/0022-indexer-in-worker.md).

children.title: Memory model ([ADR-0019](adr/0019-bounded-memory-during-indexing.md))
children.summary: This document outlines the memory model for a search index, detailing how different components are bounded and managed to ensure efficient operation. Key terms include `embed_max_tokens`, `embed_threads`, `max_file_bytes`, `max_memory_mb`, and `getChunksPage`.
children.bodyText:
## Memory model ([ADR-0019](adr/0019-bounded-memory-during-indexing.md))

| Bound | Mechanism |
| --- | --- |
| Per-text memory | `embed_max_tokens` cap, chunks split to fit |
| CPU | `embed_threads` |
| Big files | `max_file_bytes` skip |
| Host RSS | `max_memory_mb` guard (GC, wait, stop with error) |
| Startup | counts via SQL, no vector loading |
| Search / backup | paged reads (`getChunksPage`) |
| Model | out of the host, in the shared worker |

children.title: Storage layout
children.summary:
- Storage layout uses SQLite files for each project key, isolated outside the worktree.
- Brute-force cosine similarity is used for vector storage, no ANN.
- Backup is stored as sorted JSONL in the worktree and imported on start if empty.
children.bodyText:
## Storage layout

- One SQLite file set per project key, derived from the worktree
  ([ADR-0003](adr/0003-per-project-sqlite-file-isolation.md)); physically
  isolated, outside the worktree.
- `bun:sqlite` in opencode, `better-sqlite3` under Node
  ([ADR-0017](adr/0017-bun-sqlite-inside-opencode.md)).
- Brute-force cosine over `Float32` vectors, no ANN
  ([ADR-0002](adr/0002-embedded-sqlite-vector-store-over-postgres-qdrant.md)).
- Backup as sorted JSONL inside the worktree, committable and diffable;

description: This documentation summarizes the concepts and prior art for a search index plugin. It covers papers, projects, tools, and decisions related to the plugin's design and architecture. The key terms include retrieval, reasoning, code generation, and agent-driven search.

nodes.title: Concepts and prior art
nodes.summary: The plugin's ideas are derived from the original `.ai-context` stack, which shares the same research basis. The plugin adapts this design to an in-process opencode plugin, and all links are verified for availability on 2026-10-06.
nodes.bodyText:
# Concepts and prior art

Where the plugin's ideas come from. The plugin inherits most of its design
from the original `.ai-context` stack (same research basis, see that stack's
own `docs/concepts-and-prior-art.md`) and adapts it to an in-process opencode
plugin. All links below were checked for availability on 2026-10-06 (arXiv
titles verified through the arXiv API).

children.title: Papers
children.summary: This table summarizes key papers on search indexes, highlighting the main findings and where they are located within the documentation.
children.bodyText:
## Papers

| Paper | What we took from it | Where it shows up |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Agentic RAG: A Survey on Agentic RAG](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.09136) (Singh et al., 2025) | The calling agent owns the retrieval loop (which tool, when to stop). No second routing LLM. | Small tool set, `repo_structure → semantic_search → read`; [ADR-0020](adr/0020-steer-agent-to-context-tools.md) |
| [Reasoning RAG via System 1 or System 2: A Survey on Reasoning Agentic RAG](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.10408) (2025) | Retrieval and reasoning interleaved, bounded loops as a recognised pattern. | Tool descriptions state the next step and when to stop |
| [Retrieval-Augmented Code Generation: A Survey with Focus on Repository-Level Approaches](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.04905) (2025) | Multi-granularity retrieval beats single-level chunk search. | Structure (`repo_structure`), symbols/graph (`analyze_impact`), chunks (`semantic_search`) |
| [CodeRAG](https://lihui.info/doc/EMNLP25.pdf) (EMNLP 2025) | Necessity-driven retrieval, not blind top-k. | Name-precise symbol/graph lookup next to embeddings |
| [GraphCodeAgent](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.10046) | An agent navigates a structure and dependency graph itself. | `analyze_impact` over the call/import graph |
| [KGCompass](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.21710) | Narrow the search space with graph paths before the expensive step. | Structure and graph narrow the scope before reading |
| [GraphSearch](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.22009) | Dual channel (semantic + relational) issued iteratively by the agent. | `semantic_search` (chunks) next to `analyze_impact` (relations) |
| [A2RAG](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.21162) | Stop retrieval once evidence suffices. | "Stop as soon as you have enough" wording in the agent hint |
| [CodeCompass: Navigating the Navigation Paradox in Agentic Code Intelligence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.20048) | Graph navigation beats flat retrieval on architecture-heavy tasks. | Motivation for the graph; a full knowledge graph is deliberately out of scope |
| [Context-Augmented Code Generation Using Programming Knowledge Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.18251) | Fine-grained, AST-aware retrieval reduces hallucination. | AST-boundary chunking ([ADR-0013](adr/0013-web-tree-sitter-wasm-for-chunking.md)) |
| [LARGER: Lexically Anchored Repository Graph Exploration and Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.16352) | Lexical anchors into graph nodes, inside the agent's existing loop. | Keyword boost plus graph, no separate graph tool |
| [Matryoshka Representation Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.13147) | Embeddings truncatable to a prefix. | `embed_dims` truncation + re-normalise |
| [Nomic Embed: Training a Reproducible Long Context Text Embedder](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.01613) | The embedding model and its mean-pooling requirement. | [ADR-0004](adr/0004-embedding-backend-onnxruntime-node-manual-wiring.md) |

children.title: Idea → source → decision
children.summary: The documentation covers the search index's architecture and key decisions, including the use of agent-driven retrieval, hybrid vector and keyword ranking, a document tree for long Markdown, AST chunking with regex fallbacks, a call/import graph for blast radius, a local, Docker-free stack, steering the agent with descriptions and a system hint, and out-of-process embedding.
children.bodyText:
## Idea → source → decision

| Idea | Origin | Decision |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Agent drives retrieval; no router LLM | Agentic RAG surveys | ADR-0020 |
| Hybrid vector + keyword ranking | mcp-local-rag | ADR-0004 area, `keyword-rerank.ts` |
| Doc tree for long Markdown | PageIndex | ADR-0009 |
| AST chunking, regex fallbacks | Programming-KG paper, original `chunker.py` | ADR-0013, ADR-0016 |
| Call/import graph for blast radius | GraphCodeAgent, CodeCompass | ADR-0006 |
| Local, Docker-free stack | Original stack's operational cost | ADR-0001, ADR-0002 |
| Steering the agent with descriptions and a system hint | Agentic RAG, own adoption measurements | ADR-0010 (superseded in part by ADR-0020), ADR-0023 |
| Out-of-process embedding | Own memory measurements | ADR-0019, ADR-0021 |

## Deliberately not adopted

- ColBERT cross-encoder re-ranking: needs an always-on inference service,
